# STRVCT — Full Documentation

Site build: STRVCT · 2026-11-23 · 0a144bda

You write the domain model. STRVCT does the rest while the app runs: it presents your objects in a user interface on desktop and phone, stores them locally, syncs them to the cloud, imports and exports them as JSON, and lets AI agents read and edit them. Nothing is generated ahead of time: views are created from the live objects as the user navigates, and they update when the objects change. Add a property, annotate it, and every part picks it up. There is no separate form, storage mapping, or tool schema to write.

See also: llms.txt (curated index) and sitemap.xml.

Paths are relative to the site root.

<!-- Page: (root) -->
Source: ./

Write the domain model. Get the application.

**You write the domain model. STRVCT does the rest while the app runs:** it presents your objects in a user interface on desktop and phone, stores them locally, syncs them to the cloud, imports and exports them as JSON, and lets AI agents read and edit them. Nothing is generated ahead of time: views are created from the live objects as the user navigates, and they update when the objects change. Add a property, annotate it, and every part picks it up. There is no separate form, storage mapping, or tool schema to write.

**Why this hasn't worked before.** The idea is old; it's called *Naked Objects*. Its weakness was that generated interfaces looked like database forms, so real applications ended up hand-building their screens anyway.

**What's different here.** STRVCT starts from an observation: nearly every screen in an information app comes down to a few decisions about the data. What is visible? Does each item open beside its parent, as a column or tab, or sit inside it, as a section of a document? How are lists arranged? The framework handles the mechanics, including navigation and adapting to screen size. You state your choices as small hints on the model. So changing how something looks means changing a hint, not rewriting a screen.

[**Read the paper →**](docs/Naked%20Objects/index.html)

# Accessibility

Automatic, framework-level ARIA support, keyboard navigation, and preference adaptation derived from slot metadata annotations and view classes.

## Overview

STRVCT provides built-in accessibility support that works automatically for every application built on the framework. Because the UI is derived from model nodes through a small set of view classes, accessibility metadata is emitted at the framework level -- developers don't need to add ARIA attributes to individual components.

This is a direct consequence of the naked objects architecture. In a conventional web framework, accessibility is a per-component concern: every button, list, and form field needs manual ARIA attributes, and the cost scales linearly ($O(N)$) with the number of components. In STRVCT, the same $\sim$15 view classes render every application's UI, so fixing accessibility in those classes fixes it everywhere.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 280" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

  </style>

---

## Why the Naked Objects Pattern Helps

Most frameworks require developers to manually add accessibility attributes to each component. STRVCT's architecture inverts this: since the framework generates views from the model, it can also generate accessibility metadata from the model -- automatically, in one place, for all applications.

- **The slot system already describes the data:** Slot metadata maps almost directly to ARIA attributes (`description()` $\rightarrow$ `aria-description`, `isReadOnly()` $\rightarrow$ `aria-readonly`, `isRequired()` $\rightarrow$ `aria-required`).
- **JSON Schema annotations serve double duty:** The same annotations that generate JSON Schema for AI tool calls also drive accessibility attributes. A slot configured with `setMinimum(0)` and `setMaximum(100)` emits both JSON Schema constraints for AI and `aria-valuemin="0"` / `aria-valuemax="100"` for screen readers. The investment in richer slot annotations directly improves both AI integration and accessibility.
- **The node hierarchy maps to ARIA patterns:** The tile/stack navigation model (drill in, drill out, select with arrows) maps naturally to ARIA roles (`SvTilesView` $\rightarrow$ `list`, `SvTile` $\rightarrow$ `link`, `SvFieldTile` $\rightarrow$ `group`, selected tile $\rightarrow$ `aria-current`).

---

## Implementation Details

### ARIA Roles

Each core view class emits an appropriate ARIA role:

| View Class | Role | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `SvTilesView` | `list` | Container for navigable tile items |
| `SvTile` | `link` | Individual navigation item in a list |
| `SvFieldTile` | `group` | Key-value field with label and value |
| `SvBooleanFieldTile` | `checkbox` | Toggle field with checked/unchecked state |
| `SvActionFieldTile` | `button` | Clickable action |
| `SvOptionsNodeTile` | `listbox` | Container for selectable options |
| `SvOptionNodeTile` | `option` | Individual selectable option |
| `SvStackView` | `navigation` | Top-level navigation landmark |
| `SvNavView` | `region` | Named content region |
| `SvBreadCrumbsView` | `navigation` | Breadcrumb navigation with `aria-label="Breadcrumb"`; the last crumb has `aria-current="location"` |

---

## Labels and Descriptions

View classes derive ARIA labels from node metadata:

| Source | ARIA Usage | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `node.nodeAriaLabel()` | `aria-label` | `title()` by default; domain objects can override to provide a descriptive label for screen readers |
| `node.subtitle()` | `aria-description` | Subtitle text available on demand |
| `slot.description()` | `aria-description` | Detailed field-level description |
| Key view text | `aria-label` | Label on field tiles |

---

## Node-Level ARIA Overrides (`SvTitledNode`)

`SvTitledNode` provides methods that domain objects can override to customize accessibility behavior without modifying view code:

| Method | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `nodeAriaLabel()` | `title()` | Label announced by screen readers |
| `nodeAriaRole()` | `null` (view's default) | Override the view class's default ARIA role |
| `nodeAriaIsReadOnly()` | `null` (from slot editability) | Override read-only state |
| `nodeAriaIsRequired()` | `null` (from slot `isRequired()`) | Override required state |
| `nodeAriaLive()` | `null` | Returns `"polite"` or `"assertive"` for dynamic live regions |

Returning `null` defers to the view's default behavior. Returning a value overrides it. This follows the same pattern as `setNodeViewClass()` -- the framework provides sensible defaults, and the domain object overrides when it knows better.

---

## State Tracking

ARIA states are updated dynamically through the framework's notification system:
- **`aria-current`** -- Set to `"true"` on the selected tile, removed when deselected. The selected tile also receives focus.
- **`aria-checked`** -- Updated on `SvBooleanFieldTile` when the boolean value changes.
- **`aria-selected`** -- Updated on `SvOptionNodeTile` based on `isPicked()` state.
- **`aria-disabled`** -- Set on `SvActionFieldTile` when the action's node is not enabled.
- **`aria-readonly`** -- Set on `SvFieldTile` when the field is not editable.

---

## Slot Metadata to ARIA Mapping (`syncAriaFromSlotMetadata`)

`SvFieldTile` includes a `syncAriaFromSlotMetadata()` method that reads slot annotations and emits corresponding ARIA attributes:

```javascript
{
    const slot = this.newSlot("hitPoints", 0);
    slot.setSlotType("Number");
    slot.setIsRequired(true);
    slot.setAnnotation("minimum", 0);
    slot.setAnnotation("maximum", 999);
    slot.setDescription("Current character hit points");
}
```

Produces a field tile with `aria-required="true"`, `aria-valuemin="0"`, `aria-valuemax="999"`, and `aria-description="Current character hit points"` -- with no accessibility-specific code from the developer.

---

## Live Regions

- **Opt-in via nodes:** Any node can declare itself as a live region by implementing `nodeAriaLive()` returning `"polite"` or `"assertive"`. When `SvTilesView` syncs from a node with this method, it sets `aria-live` on the container.
- **Direct on chat:** `SvChatMessageTile` sets `aria-live="polite"` directly, so new chat messages and AI responses are announced to screen readers as they arrive.

---

## Focus Management & Keyboard Navigation

- **Tiles are programmatically focusable** via `tabindex="-1"`. This makes them reachable by the framework's focus management without adding them to the Tab order.
- **Focus indicators** use `:focus-visible` styling (2px solid cornflower blue outline) that appears only for keyboard navigation, not mouse clicks.
- **High contrast mode** (`prefers-contrast: more`) increases the focus outline to 3px solid white for maximum visibility.
- **Focus follows selection** -- when a tile is selected, it receives both `aria-current="true"` and DOM focus, ensuring screen readers announce the newly selected item.

---

## Visual Accessibility & Motion Preferences

- **Reduced Motion (`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`):** All animations and transitions are reduced to 0.01ms duration, iteration counts set to 1, and scroll behavior set to auto (instant).
- **High Contrast (`prefers-contrast: more`):** Focus indicators enhanced to 3px solid white with tighter offset.

---

## ARIA Landmarks

Landmark roles provide structural navigation for screen readers:
- `SvStackView` is marked as `navigation` -- the top-level navigation structure
- `SvNavView` is marked as `region` with an `aria-label` derived from the current node's title
- `SvBreadCrumbsView` is marked as `navigation` with `aria-label="Breadcrumb"`, and its last crumb as `aria-current="location"`

---

## WCAG 2.2 Compliance Matrix

| WCAG Criterion | How Addressed |
|---|---|
| **1.3.1 Info & Relationships** | ARIA roles and landmarks convey structure |
| **1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence** | DOM order matches visual order (flexbox layout) |
| **2.1.1 Keyboard** | Arrow keys, Enter, Escape for full navigation |
| **2.3.3 Animation from Interactions** | `prefers-reduced-motion` media query |
| **2.4.1 Bypass Blocks** | Landmark roles enable skip navigation |
| **2.4.6 Headings & Labels** | `aria-label` from node `title()` |
| **2.4.7 Focus Visible** | `:focus-visible` outline styling |
| **3.2.1 On Focus** | No context changes on focus |
| **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value** | ARIA roles, labels, and states on all interactive elements |

---

## Files Modifying Accessibility

| File | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| `_css.css` | `:focus-visible` styling, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast` |
| `SvTilesView.js` | `role="list"`, `aria-label`, opt-in `aria-live` |
| `SvTile.js` | `role="link"`, `tabindex="-1"`, `aria-label`, `aria-description`, `aria-current` |
| `SvFieldTile.js` | `role="group"`, `aria-label`, `aria-readonly`, `syncAriaFromSlotMetadata()` |
| `SvBooleanFieldTile.js` | `role="checkbox"`, `aria-checked` |
| `SvActionFieldTile.js` | `role="button"`, `aria-label`, `aria-disabled` |
| `SvOptionsNodeTile.js` | `role="listbox"` |
| `SvOptionNodeTile.js` | `role="option"`, `aria-selected` |
| `SvChatMessageTile.js` | `aria-live="polite"` |
| `SvStackView.js` | `role="navigation"` |
| `SvNavView.js` | `role="region"`, `aria-label` |
| `SvBreadCrumbsView.js` | `role="navigation"`, `aria-label="Breadcrumb"`, `aria-current="location"` |

---

# Comparing to React

A guide to Strvct for developers who know React.

## The Short Version

React and Strvct start from opposite ends. React starts from the view: you write the screens, and the model, storage, and sync are yours to connect. Strvct starts from the model: you write the domain objects, and the screens, storage, and sync are derived from them.

React is a view library. You write the screens as components, and you choose and connect the rest yourself: state stores, forms, routing, persistence, and any tools you give an AI agent.

Strvct is a model-first framework. You write the domain model as classes with annotated properties (**slots**). The framework builds the rest from that model: the screens, navigation, local storage, cloud sync, JSON import and export, and an interface agents can use to read and edit the data.

In a typical React stack, adding one field to a record touches about five places: a database migration, an ORM model, an API schema, a state store, and a form component. In Strvct, you add one slot declaration.

---

## One Record, Both Ways

### React

```jsx
// ContactForm.jsx
function ContactForm({ contactId, onSave }) {
    const [name, setName] = useState("");
    const [email, setEmail] = useState("");

    useEffect(() => {
        api.getContact(contactId).then(data => {
            setName(data.name);
            setEmail(data.email);
        });
    }, [contactId]);

    const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        await api.updateContact(contactId, { name, email });
        onSave();
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
            <label>Name: <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} /></label>
            <label>Email: <input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} /></label>
            <button type="submit">Save</button>
        </form>
    );
}
```

This is just the form. The API endpoints, the database schema, the route that reaches this screen, and the list screen that links to it are all separate.

### Strvct

```javascript
// Contact.js
(class Contact extends SvStorableNode {

    initPrototypeSlots () {
        {
            const slot = this.newSlot("name", "");
            slot.setSlotType("String");
            slot.setShouldStoreSlot(true);   // saved locally, synced to the cloud
            slot.setSyncsToView(true);       // the UI updates when it changes
            slot.setCanEditInspection(true); // shown as an editable field
        }
        {
            const slot = this.newSlot("email", "");
            slot.setSlotType("String");
            slot.setShouldStoreSlot(true);
            slot.setSyncsToView(true);
            slot.setCanEditInspection(true);
        }
    }

    initPrototype () {
        this.setTitle("Contact");
        this.setShouldStore(true);
    }

}.initThisClass());
```

This is the whole thing. A `Contacts` collection holding these objects gets a list, a detail view with editable fields, navigation between them, storage, and sync. There is no save button, because every edit is committed at the end of the event loop.

---

## Concept Map

| In React | In Strvct | The difference |
|---|---|---|
| Component (JSX) | A view derived from the node, or a custom view class | Views are created at runtime, as the user navigates, from the node and its slots. |
| `useState` | A slot, read with `name()` and set with `setName(v)` | State lives on model objects, not in components. |
| Context, Redux, Zustand | The object graph itself | There is one model. Views observe it, and nothing copies it into a store. |
| `useEffect` | A notification observation, or a `didUpdateSlot<Name>()` method | Declaring `didUpdateSlotEmail()` is the subscription. Observations are weak, so there is nothing to unsubscribe. |
| React Router | The navigation path through the object graph | A screen is a path of nodes, so there is no route table to maintain. |
| TanStack Query, REST, an ORM | Object pools in IndexedDB, synced to the cloud | Changed objects are marked dirty and committed in a batch. |
| TypeScript, PropTypes | Slot types, checked at runtime | The same type information validates setters, imported JSON, and agent patches. |
| Tool definitions for an LLM | A generic schema-and-patch interface | Agents read a class's schema and send JSON patches. Adding a class adds no tools. |

---

## How Screens Are Decided

In React you design each screen. In Strvct, a screen comes from a few decisions about the model, which you state as hints on the node class:

- **Beside or inside.** When you open a child, does it get its own column or tab beside its parent, or is it drawn inside the parent as a section of a document? The default is a column. `nodeChildrenLayout()` returning `"inline"` shows the next levels in place as a document, `"grid"` lays the children out as a wrapping gallery of cells, and `nodeSubnodesAreAnchoredTabs()` shows children as tabs that open side by side when there is room.
- **What shows.** A node can present a different node in its place with `nodePresentedNode()`. For example, a character can present a readable character sheet built from its data.
- **How items look.** Hints such as `nodeTileLayout()` and `nodeChildrenTileWidth()` name a role, like `"status"` or `"roster"`, and the theme decides what that role looks like.

The framework takes care of the mechanics: the navigation path, collapsing columns into a stack on a phone, turning side-by-side panes into tabs when space runs out, editing in place, and keyboard and screen-reader support. A layout change is usually a one-line hint, not a new screen.

---

## How State Flows

**React:** A state change re-renders the component subtree. React diffs the new virtual DOM against the old one and patches the real DOM. To persist the change, you add an effect, a mutation hook, or a sync layer.

**Strvct:** A view calls a setter on the model. The setter updates the slot, marks the object dirty for storage, and posts a notification. At the end of the event loop, the sync scheduler merges duplicate updates, and each observing view reads the new values from its node. Nothing is diffed, and persistence is part of the same step.

The model never refers to views. Because of this, the same model code runs under Node.js with no browser, so domain tests don't need jsdom or a headless browser.

---

## When the Generated UI Isn't Enough

Everyone asks this first: what happens when I need a kanban board, a canvas, or a layout that doesn't follow the object hierarchy?

The answer comes in steps, from least code to most:

1. **Use an existing hint.** Many "custom" layouts turn out to be an inline document, a set of anchored tabs, or a presented node.
2. **Add a new hint.** If a look is missing, add a hint that names the role and teach the generic view to read it. Every node can use it after that, and it follows the theme.
3. **Write a custom view.** For genuinely custom drawing, such as a canvas, a map, or a board, write a view class. Views are found by name: a `Contact` node uses a `ContactView` if one exists. You can also name the class with `nodeViewClassName()`. The view observes the node and calls its methods, and everything else in the app stays generated.

A custom view is simpler to write here than a React component, and simpler for a coding agent to write too. The data contract already exists: the node's slots, their types, and its notifications. The view doesn't fetch, cache, or store anything. It reads the node, draws, and calls methods on the node. Its scope is limited to the one node it replaces, and it can still hand that node's children back to the generated views.

The cost is real, though. A custom view is UI that is no longer derived from the model, so it doesn't follow theme changes automatically and you maintain it by hand. That is why it is the last step, not the first.

---

## Trade-offs

**What you give up with Strvct:**

- **The ecosystem.** Strvct doesn't use npm in the browser or React component libraries. Third-party code is vendored as source. You won't find a shadcn/ui or MUI equivalent.
- **Control over every screen.** You shape screens through the model and hints. If your product is mainly a sequence of designed screens, such as a landing page, a storefront, or a branded onboarding flow, you will be working against the framework.
- **SEO.** There is no server-side rendering. The UI is built in the browser.
- **The style.** Strvct uses classes, mutable objects, and declared slots. If you are used to functional components and hooks, it will take some adjustment.

**What you get:**

- One model drives the UI, storage, sync, exchange, and agent access, so they can't drift apart.
- Local-first by default: the app works offline and syncs when it can.
- An AI interface that doesn't grow with the model. Agents read schemas and send patches, and a rejected patch can return the slot's schema so the agent can correct itself.
- Domain tests that run under plain Node.js.

**Strvct fits** structured-information apps: CRMs, project and issue trackers, editors for structured documents, settings panels, admin tools, game tools, and apps where people and AI agents work on the same data.

**React fits** apps where the screens are the product: marketing sites, storefronts, media-heavy pages, and anything that depends on SEO or on a specific component library.

# Annotations

One slot declaration carries metadata that independent framework layers read without coordinating. Adding a new layer leaves existing layers unchanged.

# Diagram Conventions

Style and layout rules for the SVG diagrams used throughout the Strvct docs.

## Why a Convention

The docs use ~30 inline SVG diagrams to visualize architecture, flows, and relationships. Without a shared style they drift apart, become harder to scan, and require per-page mental re-orientation. The rules below let any diagram be authored, edited, or scripted against the same set of expectations.

## Style Block

Every diagram opens with the same `<style>` block:

```svg
<style>
  text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
  .b { font-weight: 600; }
  .dim { fill: #666; }
  .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
  .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
  .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  .flow-dashed { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; stroke-dasharray: 4 3; }
</style>
```

- **`.b`** — bold text (titles, labels)
- **`.dim`** — secondary text (descriptions, captions); color `#666`
- **`.box`** — outline rectangle, no fill; used for outer containers
- **`.fill`** — cream-filled rectangle (`#f0ede5`); used for inner content blocks
- **`.flow`** — solid line for direct references / calls / direct data flow
- **`.flow-dashed`** — dashed line (`4 3`) for indirect notifications, observers, no-direct-reference relationships

## Arrowhead Markers

A single arrowhead marker is defined per diagram in `<defs>`, with a unique id (e.g., `ato`, `aio`, `anc`):

```svg
<defs>
  <marker id="xxx" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
    <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
  </marker>
</defs>
```

Lines reference it via `marker-end="url(#xxx)"`.

## ViewBox

- **Width**: 820 (matches the docs column width)
- **Height**: tight to content with ~20px bottom margin below the last element

## Layout Rules

### Inside fill rects

Content is **left-top justified** with consistent padding:

- **Text x** = `fill.x + 15` (15px left padding)
- **First text baseline y** = `fill.y + 20`
- **Subsequent lines** spaced 18px apart
- **Bottom padding** = 11px (cap-top above first baseline matches descender-bottom below last baseline). Concretely: `fill.h = (last_text_y - fill.y) + 14`.

### Stacking fill rects

Vertically adjacent fill rects in the same column should sit **15px apart** when they're sibling rows in a list. Larger gaps (~30px) are appropriate when an arrow + label lives between them.

For centered stacks (rects whose horizontal centers align around `viewBox.width / 2`), give all rects the same width — use the maximum needed by any row's content, centered.

### Inside .box containers

Containers wrap one or more `.fill` rects plus optional title/subtitle text and caption text below the fills.

- **Container title (b)** at `container.x + 15`, `container.y + 22`
- **Container subtitle (dim)** at `container.x + 15`, `container.y + 42` (when present)
- **Inner fills** at `container.x + 15`, `container.y + 60+` (with 15px horizontal padding from container edges)
- **Captions below last fill** are left-justified at `container.x + 15`, starting at `last_fill_bottom + 24`, with 18px line spacing
- **Container bottom padding** = 15px below the lowest content element

### Multi-column layouts

For 2- and 3-column comparisons, each column's containers should be the same width and aligned at the top (`y=20`). Container heights should match (use the tallest column's height). Captions inside columns are still left-justified to their column.

## Lines and Arrows

- **Solid line** (`.flow`) — direct reference or call (e.g., a UI view calling getter/setter on its model node)
- **Dashed line** (`.flow-dashed`) — indirect notification or observation (e.g., the model posts a notification, observers pick it up without holding a reference)
- **Arrow direction** points to the *recipient* of the action

For the Model ↔ UI ↔ Storage triple, mutation notifications from Model outward are **dashed** (Model holds no references); UI/Storage calls into Model are **solid** (they hold direct references).

## Two-line Arrow Labels

When labeling a line in a tight gap:

- **For label above the line**: two text elements at `arrow_y - 22` and `arrow_y - 7`
- **For label below the line**: two text elements at `arrow_y + 13` and `arrow_y + 28`
- All centered with `text-anchor="middle"` at the gap midpoint x

## Captions and Footnotes

The summary line below a diagram is **left-justified** at the same x as the leftmost container (when there is one) or `container.x + 15`. Do not center such lines.

## When to Break the Conventions

The conventions exist to keep diagrams scannable, not to be rigid. Acceptable deviations:

- A diagram showing a state machine or a network graph won't use stacked fills at all
- A side-by-side comparison may need asymmetric heights when content lengths differ enough that padding the shorter side would look strange
- Inline annotations (e.g., a small "(weak ref)" label between two boxes) can sit at any x

When in doubt, prefer consistency with adjacent diagrams in the same page or section.

# Persistence Pipeline

Drilling into Local Storage. The object pool persists slot mutations through the synchronous track on the left. The blob pool stores content-addressable binaries asynchronously on the right. Garbage collection bridges them: the object pool walks reachable nodes, collects referenced hashes, and the blob pool removes any blob not in that set.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 450" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <style>

    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>
  <defs>
    <marker id="a6" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- Left Column: Object Pool & Record Store -->
  <rect class="box" x="40" y="20" width="350" height="410"/>
  <text x="55" y="42" class="b">Object Pool &amp; Record Store (Synchronous)</text>

# View ↔ Model ↔ Storage Syncing

A user or agent mutation is validated by the setter, then broadcast through the notification center. View and storage layers schedule their work end-of-event-loop.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 520" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>

    <marker id="a3" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

# View Resolution

When a node becomes visible, the framework finds a view class by climbing the node's inheritance chain. Custom views are an override; the default is always available.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 330" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <style>
    text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>
  <defs>

# Events and Gestures

Event flow, listeners, gesture recognizers, timers, keyboard handling, and drag-and-drop.

STRVCT provides two layers for handling user interaction: **event listeners** that wrap native DOM events and forward them to handler methods on views, and **gesture recognizers** that interpret sequences of events as higher-level gestures like taps, pans, and pinches. A managed **timer system** supports deferred work with both strong and GC-friendly weak timeouts.

Most application code uses gesture recognizers rather than raw event listeners. The gesture system unifies mouse and touch input, handles multi-touch emulation on desktop, and coordinates competing gestures through a global `SvGestureManager`.

  
    text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  
  
    
      
    
  
  
  Browser DOM Event
  mousedown, touchstart, keydown, drop, ...
  - 
  
  SvEventListener
  wraps a DOM event; calls a named method
  on the delegate view (e.g. onMouseDown)
  - 
  if a gesture recognizer is attached
  
  SvGestureRecognizer  ·  optional layer
  state machine consumes raw events;
  SvGestureManager arbitrates competing gestures;
  sends onGestureBegin / Move / Complete to view
  - 
  
  View Handler
  application logic runs
  For raw events without gestures, the listener calls the view's handler method directly, skipping the gesture layer.

- [Event Flow](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Event%20Flow/index.html) — The end-to-end path from a browser event to an application handler.
- [Event Listeners](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Event%20Listeners/index.html) — Thin wrappers around native DOM events that forward to handler methods on views.
- [Gesture Recognizers](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Gesture%20Recognizers/index.html) — Higher-level state machines that interpret sequences of events as meaningful gestures.
- [Timers](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Timers/index.html) — Managed timeout system for scheduling deferred work, with support for weak references to avoid preventing garbage collection.
- [Keyboard and Focus](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Keyboard%20and%20Focus/index.html) — Keyboard state tracking, modifier-aware key dispatch, and the responder chain for focus management.
- [Drag and Drop](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Drag%20and%20Drop/index.html) — Browser drag-and-drop support for views and nodes, covering drop targets, drag sources, and MIME-type dispatch.

<!-- Page: docs/Events and Gestures/Drag and Drop -->
Source: docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Drag%20and%20Drop/

# Drag and Drop

Browser drag-and-drop support for views and nodes, covering drop targets, drag sources, and MIME-type dispatch.

## Overview

The browser's native HTML5 drag-and-drop API is low-level and inconsistent—you must manually parse `DataTransfer` objects, handle files versus text strings differently, prevent default browser navigation on dropped files, and manage empty-space drops that bypass child elements.

STRVCT wraps this into a clean, declarative protocol:
- **Drop Targets:** Views register to accept dropped content (`setIsRegisteredForBrowserDrop(true)`). Dropped data arrives pre-parsed, typed by MIME, and dispatched directly to a handler method named by convention.
- **Drag Sources:** Views register as draggable sources (`setIsRegisteredForBrowserDrag(true)`), populating `DataTransfer` payloads when a drag initiates.

    .b { font-weight: 600; }

    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>

      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="20" width="380" height="52"/>

---

## Key Framework Classes

| File / Class Name | Purpose & Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| `SvDomView_browserDragAndDrop.js` | Category on `SvDomView` implementing drop/drag target APIs. |
| `SvDropListener.js` | Manages element drop event listeners (`dragenter`, `dragover`, `dragleave`, `drop`). |
| `SvDragListener.js` | Manages element drag source event listeners (`dragstart`, `dragend`). |
| `SvDocumentBody.js` | Global drop prevention on `document.body` to stop browser file navigation. |

---

## Drop Targets API

### 1. Registering a View for Drops
```javascript
init () {
    super.init();
    this.setIsRegisteredForBrowserDrop(true); // Attaches SvDropListener
    return this;
}
```

### 2. Accepting or Rejecting Drops
Override `acceptsDrop(event)` to inspect incoming transfer types:

```javascript
acceptsDrop (event) {
    // Inspect event.dataTransfer.types
    return event.dataTransfer.types.includes("text/plain");
}
```

### 3. MIME Type Method Dispatch (`dropMethodForMimeType`)

| MIME Type | Convention Handler Method Name |
|---|---|
| `text/plain` | `onBrowserDropTextPlain(dataChunk)` |
| `text/html` | `onBrowserDropTextHtml(dataChunk)` |
| `image/png` | `onBrowserDropImagePng(dataChunk)` |
| `image/jpeg` | `onBrowserDropImageJpeg(dataChunk)` |
| `application/json` | `onBrowserDropApplicationJson(dataChunk)` |

### 4. Data Chunk Object (`SvDataUrl`)
Dropped payloads are wrapped in an `SvDataUrl` instance (`dataChunk`):
- `dataChunk.mimeType()`: Returns the MIME type string.
- `dataChunk.decodedData()`: Returns the decoded string or JSON content.
- `dataChunk.setDataUrlString(url)`: Contains the data URL string for dropped files.

### 5. Visual Drag Highlighting
Override styling hooks for hover feedback:
```javascript
dragHighlight () {
    this.setBorder("2px dashed cornflowerblue");
}

dragUnhighlight () {
    this.setBorder("none");
}
```

---

## Drag Sources API

To make a view draggable:

```javascript
init () {
    super.init();
    this.setIsRegisteredForBrowserDrag(true);
    return this;
}

// Populate transfer payload on drag start
onBrowserDragStart (event) {
    const dt = event.dataTransfer;
    dt.setData("text/plain", this.node().title());
    dt.setData("application/json", JSON.stringify(this.node().asJson()));
}
```

- [Keyboard and Focus](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Keyboard%20and%20Focus/index.html): Modifier-aware key routing.

# Event Flow

The end-to-end path from a browser event to an application handler.

## Overview

Raw DOM events are too low-level for most application code. Distinguishing a tap from a long-press from a pan requires tracking timing, movement thresholds, and finger counts — and when multiple gestures compete on the same element, the browser offers no arbitration. STRVCT's event pipeline absorbs this complexity: raw events feed into gesture recognizer state machines, a central SvGestureManager resolves conflicts (so a tap and a long-press on the same view don't both fire), and the application only sees clean, high-level callbacks like `onTapComplete` or `onPanMove`. Views that don't need gestures can still handle raw events directly — the gesture layer is additive, not mandatory.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 540" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <style>
    text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>
  <defs>
    <marker id="aef" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="20" width="380" height="52"/>
  <text x="235" y="40" class="b">1. Browser DOM Event</text>
  <text x="235" y="58" class="dim">mouse, touch, keyboard, drop, ...</text>
  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="72" x2="410" y2="110" marker-end="url(#aef)"/>
  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="110" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="130" class="b">2. SvEventListener</text>
  <text x="235" y="148" class="dim">calls named method on delegate view;</text>
  <text x="235" y="166" class="dim">returning false stops propagation</text>
  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="180" x2="410" y2="215" marker-end="url(#aef)"/>
  <text x="425" y="202" class="dim">if a gesture recognizer is attached</text>
  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="215" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="235" class="b">3. Recognizer state machine updates</text>
  <text x="235" y="253" class="dim">tracks finger count, timing, movement;</text>
  <text x="235" y="271" class="dim">requests activation when conditions are met</text>
  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="285" x2="410" y2="320" marker-end="url(#aef)"/>
  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="320" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="340" class="b">4. SvGestureManager arbitrates</text>
  <text x="235" y="358" class="dim">resolves competing gestures across views;</text>
  <text x="235" y="376" class="dim">if accepted, sends delegate messages</text>
  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="390" x2="410" y2="425" marker-end="url(#aef)"/>
  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="425" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="445" class="b">5. View handler executes</text>
  <text x="235" y="463" class="dim">onGestureBegin / Move / Complete / Cancelled,</text>
  <text x="235" y="481" class="dim">or raw onMouseDown, etc., for non-gesture events</text>
  <text x="410" y="525" text-anchor="middle" class="dim">For raw event listeners (no gesture), steps 3 and 4 are skipped; the listener calls the view handler directly at step 2.</text>
</svg>


For raw event listeners (without gestures), the handler is called directly on the view at step 2, skipping the gesture layer.

## Detailed Steps

1. **Browser fires a native DOM event** (mouse, touch, keyboard, etc.) on a DOM element.

2. **An `SvEventListener` receives it.** The listener was registered on the view's element via `addEventListener()`. It calls the corresponding method on its delegate — typically the view itself. For example, a `mousedown` event calls `onMouseDown(event)` on the view.

3. **Returning `false` stops propagation.** If the handler returns `false`, `event.stopPropagation()` is called, preventing the event from bubbling to ancestor elements.

4. **Gesture recognizers observe the event.** If the view has gesture recognizers attached, they receive the raw event and update their internal state machines. For example, a `SvTapGestureRecognizer` tracks mousedown/mouseup timing and position.

5. **The recognizer requests activation.** When the gesture's conditions are met (correct finger count, sufficient movement, hold duration, etc.), it calls `SvGestureManager.requestActiveGesture()`.

6. **SvGestureManager arbitrates.** The singleton manager checks whether another gesture is already active, considers the view hierarchy, and decides whether to accept or reject the request. Competing gestures on the same or ancestor views are cancelled.

7. **The recognizer sends delegate messages.** If accepted, the recognizer calls phase methods on the view: `onGestureBegin`, `onGestureMove`, `onGestureComplete`, or `onGestureCancelled`.

8. **The view executes application logic.** The handler method runs whatever the application needs — updating model state, triggering animations, navigating, etc.

## Special Cases

- **Keyboard events** route through `SvKeyboard`, which generates modifier-aware method names (e.g., `onShiftAKeyDown`).
- **Drag-and-drop events** route through `SvDropListener`/`SvDragListener` and the MIME dispatch chain in `SvDomView_browserDragAndDrop`.
- **Focus events** interact with the responder chain in `SvResponderDomView`.


---

<!-- Page: docs/Events and Gestures/Event Listeners -->
Source: docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Event%20Listeners/

# Event Listeners

Thin wrappers around native DOM events that forward to handler methods on views.

## Architecture

Calling `addEventListener` directly ties views to specific DOM event names and requires manual bookkeeping — tracking which listeners are registered, removing them at the right time, and ensuring handlers exist before registering. Event listeners centralize this: they register lazily on first use, group related events (e.g., all mouse events) into a single toggle, dispatch to named methods on the view, and clean up automatically when the view is retired. This keeps views focused on handling events rather than managing listener lifecycle.

Event listening is built on two base classes:

- **`SvEventListener`** — Wraps a single DOM event. Registers with a target element, and when the event fires, calls a named method on its delegate (typically the view).
- **`SvEventSetListener`** — Groups related `SvEventListener` instances. Subclasses define which events they cover via `setupListeners()`.

Views manage their listeners through `SvListenerDomView`, which maintains a map of listener class names to listener instances. Listeners are created lazily on first access and cleaned up when the view is removed.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 380" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <style>
    text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>

## Available Listeners

| Listener | Events |
|----------|--------|
| `SvMouseListener` | mousedown, mouseup, mouseover, mouseleave, click, dblclick, contextmenu |
| `SvMouseMoveListener` | mousemove (separate to avoid overhead when not needed) |
| `SvTouchListener` | touchstart, touchmove, touchcancel, touchend |
| `SvTouchMoveListener` | touchmove (separate for same reason) |
| `SvKeyboardListener` | keydown, keyup, input |
| `SvFocusListener` | focus, blur, focusin, focusout |
| `SvDragListener` | dragstart, drag, dragend |
| `SvDropListener` | dragenter, dragover, dragleave, drop |
| `SvScrollListener` | scroll |
| `SvWheelListener` | wheel |
| `SvClipboardListener` | copy, cut, paste |
| `SvSelectListener` | select |
| `SvWindowListener` | resize |
| `SvAnimationListener` | animationstart, animationend, animationiteration |
| `SvTransitionListener` | transitionend |
| `SvGamePadListener` | gamepadconnected, gamepaddisconnected |

## Registering for Events

Views provide convenience methods for common event families:

```javascript
view.setIsRegisteredForMouse(true);    // onMouseDown, onMouseUp, etc.
view.setIsRegisteredForKeyboard(true); // onKeyDown, onKeyUp
view.setIsRegisteredForFocus(true);    // onFocus, onBlur
view.setIsRegisteredForClicks(true);   // uses a SvTapGestureRecognizer internally
view.setIsRegisteredForWindowResize(true);
view.setIsRegisteredForBrowserDrop(true);
```

Event handler methods are called by name on the view. Returning `false` from a handler calls `event.stopPropagation()` to prevent the event from bubbling.

## Listener Lifecycle

Listeners are created lazily when first accessed via `SvListenerDomView.listenerNamed()`:

```javascript
listenerNamed (className) {
    const map = this.eventListenersMap();
    if (!map.has(className)) {
        const instance = Object.getClassNamed(className).clone()
            .setListenTarget(this.element())
            .setDelegate(this);
        map.set(className, instance);
    }
    return map.get(className);
}
```

The listener target is the view's DOM element. The delegate is the view itself.

`SvEventSetListener.start()` iterates its child `SvEventListener` instances, each of which:

1. Checks `delegateCanRespond()` — verifies the delegate has the handler method
2. Calls `addEventListener()` on the target element with the configured options

`stop()` removes all event listeners. `setIsListening(bool)` toggles between started and stopped states.

If the listen target, delegate, or capture mode changes while listening, the listener automatically stops, updates its configuration, and restarts via `resync()`.

## Cleanup

Listeners are automatically removed when a view is retired from the hierarchy. The view's `prepareToRetire()` calls `removeAllListeners()`, which stops every registered `SvEventSetListener` and clears the listener map. No manual cleanup is needed for views that follow normal lifecycle patterns.


---

<!-- Page: docs/Events and Gestures/Gesture Recognizers -->
Source: docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Gesture%20Recognizers/

# Gesture Recognizers

Higher-level state machines that interpret sequences of events as meaningful gestures.

## Unified Input Architecture

The browser provides two separate event families for pointing—mouse events on desktop and touch events on mobile—with different semantics, coordinate systems, and lifecycle patterns. Without an abstraction layer, every interactive view needs parallel code paths for both input types, plus logic to prevent ghost clicks and handle edge cases where both fire simultaneously.

Gesture recognizers eliminate this complexity:
- They consume raw mouse and touch events internally and present a single, input-agnostic interface to the view.
- A `SvPanGestureRecognizer` works identically whether driven by a mouse drag or a finger swipe—the view implements `onPanBegin` once and it works on every device.
- New interaction features are automatically cross-platform from the first line of code, with no per-device testing or branching required.

Mouse input naturally supports single-finger gestures (tap, pan, long-press, slide). Multi-finger gestures (pinch, rotation) require touch input or desktop Shift-click multi-touch emulation.

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 520" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <style>
    text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>
  <defs>
    <marker id="agr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="20" width="380" height="52"/>
  <text x="235" y="40" class="b">1. Raw Mouse / Touch Input Stream</text>
  <text x="235" y="58" class="dim">Unified input abstraction</text>

  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="72" x2="410" y2="110" marker-end="url(#agr)"/>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="110" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="130" class="b">2. SvGestureRecognizer State Machine</text>
  <text x="235" y="148" class="dim">Tracks finger count, timing, movement, hold;</text>
  <text x="235" y="166" class="dim">Tap, Pan, Pinch, Rotation, LongPress, Slide</text>

  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="180" x2="410" y2="225" marker-end="url(#agr)"/>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="225" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="245" class="b">3. SvGestureManager Singleton Arbitration</text>
  <text x="235" y="263" class="dim">Arbitrates competing gestures;</text>
  <text x="235" y="281" class="dim">Cancels conflicts across view hierarchy</text>

  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="295" x2="410" y2="340" marker-end="url(#agr)"/>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="340" width="380" height="88"/>
  <text x="235" y="360" class="b">4. Delegate Phase Messages Sent to View</text>
  <text x="235" y="378" class="dim">onGestureBegin → onGestureMove → onGestureComplete</text>
  <text x="235" y="396" class="dim">(or onGestureCancelled if interrupted)</text>

  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="428" x2="410" y2="475" marker-end="url(#agr)"/>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="475" width="380" height="34"/>
  <text x="235" y="495" class="b">5. Application Handler Executes</text>
</svg>

---

## How Gestures Work

A gesture recognizer is a state machine attached to a view via `addGestureRecognizer()`. When gesture conditions are met, the recognizer sends delegate messages to the view:

```
acceptsGestureType(gesture)     — Optional: can the view accept this gesture?
onGestureTypeBegin(gesture)     — Gesture recognized and started
onGestureTypeMove(gesture)      — Gesture in progress
onGestureTypeComplete(gesture)  — Gesture completed successfully
onGestureTypeCancelled(gesture) — Gesture interrupted or cancelled
```

---

## Complete Gesture Recognizers Suite

| Recognizer Class | Detects | Primary Configuration Settors |
|---|---|---|
| **`SvTapGestureRecognizer`** | Single or multi-tap | `setNumberOfTapsRequired()`, `setNumberOfFingersRequired()`, `setMaxHoldPeriod()` |
| **`SvPanGestureRecognizer`** | Click-and-drag panning | `setMinNumberOfFingersRequired()`, `setMaxNumberOfFingersAllowed()` |
| **`SvPinchGestureRecognizer`** | Two-finger pinch/zoom | Fixed to 2 fingers |
| **`SvRotationGestureRecognizer`** | Two-finger rotation | Fixed to 2 fingers |
| **`SvLongPressGestureRecognizer`** | Press-and-hold gesture | `setTimePeriod()` (default 500ms) |
| **`SvSlideGestureRecognizer`** | Directional slide | `setDirection("left"|"right"|"up"|"down")`, `setMaxPerpendicularDistToBegin()` |
| **`SvEdgePanGestureRecognizer`** | Pan starting at view edge | Subclasses for left, right, top, bottom edges |
| **`SvScreenEdgePan`** | Pan starting at screen boundary | Subclasses for left, right, top, bottom screen boundaries |

---

## Adding Gestures & Convenience API

```javascript
// Convenience methods on SvDomView
view.addDefaultTapGesture();       // Single tap
view.addDefaultDoubleTapGesture(); // Double tap
view.addDefaultPanGesture();       // Drag panning

// Custom recognizer configuration
const gesture = SvLongPressGestureRecognizer.clone();
gesture.setTimePeriod(800); // 800ms hold requirement
view.addGestureRecognizer(gesture);

// View implements callback handler
onLongPressComplete (gesture) {
    this.openContextMenu();
}
```

---

## Global Arbitration (`SvGestureManager`)

`SvGestureManager` is a singleton that coordinates competing gestures globally across the entire view tree:
- **Priority & Hierarchy:** Child views can steal control from parent views.
- **Active Lock:** Once a gesture is accepted, competing gestures on the same or ancestor views are automatically cancelled.
- **Explicit Cancellation:** Views can cancel gestures programmatically: `view.cancelAllGesturesExcept(panGesture)`.

---

## Cleanup, Teardown & Memory Safety

When a view is retired and unmounted from the DOM hierarchy, `prepareToRetire()` executes a 3-step cleanup pipeline:

1. **`removeAllGestureRecognizers()`:** Stops each recognizer, removes DOM listeners, and clears the view target.
2. **`removeAllListeners()`:** Unbinds all element-level DOM event listeners.
3. **`cancelAllTimeouts()`:** Clears any pending gesture hold timers.

### Weak Reference Timers:
Gesture recognizers use **`addWeakTimeout()`** for internal hold delays. `addWeakTimeout()` holds only a `WeakRef` to the view target, enabling unmounted views to be reclaimed cleanly by JavaScript's garbage collector without timer leaks.

---

## Multi-Touch Desktop Emulation

On desktop browsers, holding **Shift** while clicking simulates a second touch point. This allows testing multi-finger pinch, zoom, and rotation gestures using a standard mouse.

---

## Related Guides

- [Drag and Drop](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Drag%20and%20Drop/index.html): HTML5 drag-and-drop MIME dispatch.
- [Keyboard and Focus](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Keyboard%20and%20Focus/index.html): Modifier-aware key routing.

<!-- Page: docs/Events and Gestures/Keyboard and Focus -->
Source: docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Keyboard%20and%20Focus/

# Keyboard and Focus

Keyboard state tracking, modifier-aware key dispatch, and the responder chain for focus management.

## Overview

The browser's native keyboard handling has two critical gaps:
1. `keydown` and `keyup` events tell you which key was pressed, but not which other keys are currently held.
2. DOM `focus` is element-level without a concept of a view hierarchy responder chain or tab-order routing between custom view containers.

STRVCT addresses both:
- **`SvKeyboard` Singleton:** Tracks global keyboard state and generates **modifier-aware method names** (e.g. `onShiftAKeyDown`, `onAlternate_D_KeyDown`).
- **`SvResponderDomView`:** Layers a responder chain on top of DOM focus to manage focus acquisition, loss, and Tab-key navigation through the view tree.

    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .flow { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
  </style>
  <defs>
    <marker id="akf" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#111"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="20" width="380" height="52"/>
  <text x="235" y="40" class="b">1. Raw keydown Event</text>

  <line class="flow" x1="410" y1="72" x2="410" y2="115" marker-end="url(#akf)"/>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="115" width="380" height="70"/>
  <text x="235" y="135" class="b">2. SvKeyboard Singleton</text>
  <text x="235" y="153" class="dim">Tracks currently pressed keys &amp; modifiers;</text>
  <text x="235" y="171" class="dim">Builds method name: "onShiftAKeyDown"</text>

  <rect class="fill" x="220" y="355" width="380" height="52"/>
  <text x="235" y="375" class="b">4. view.onShiftAKeyDown(event) Runs</text>
  <text x="235" y="393" class="dim">View-specific key handler executes</text>

  <text x="410" y="445" text-anchor="middle" class="dim">Views handle specific key combinations by implementing named methods; no modifier-flag parsing required.</text>
</svg>

---

## Modifier-Aware Method Naming Pattern

When a key event fires, `SvKeyboard` generates a method name following the pattern:

```
on[Modifiers][KeyName]Key[Down|Up]
```

### Examples:
- Pressing **A** with **Shift**: `onShiftAKeyDown(event)`
- Pressing **D** with **Option/Alt** and **Shift**: `onAlternate_D_KeyDown(event)` (toggles Developer Mode)
- Pressing **Enter**: `onEnterKeyDown(event)`
- Pressing **Escape**: `onEscapeKeyDown(event)`

---

## Platform Modifier Mappings

- **macOS:** Command key maps to `MetaLeft` / `MetaRight` (`onMetaKey...`). Option key maps to `Alternate` (`onAlternateKey...`).
- **Windows / Linux:** Control key maps to `Control` (`onControlKey...`). Alt key maps to `Alternate` (`onAlternateKey...`).

---

## Responder Chain (`SvResponderDomView`)

`SvResponderDomView` provides focus management methods across the view tree:

- **`acceptsFirstResponder()`:** Returns `true` if the view can receive keyboard focus.
- **`becomeFirstResponder()`:** Acquires focus, updates styling, and calls `willBecomeFirstResponder()`.
- **`releaseFirstResponder()`:** Releases focus and calls `willReleaseFirstResponder()`.
- **`nextKeyView`:** References the next view in the tab order, enabling Tab key navigation across view inputs.

---

## Related Guides

- [Gesture Recognizers](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Gesture%20Recognizers/index.html): Touch and mouse gesture state machines.
- [Drag and Drop](docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Drag%20and%20Drop/index.html): HTML5 drag-and-drop MIME dispatch.

Source: docs/Events%20and%20Gestures/Timers/

# Timers

Managed timeout system for scheduling deferred work, with support for weak references to avoid preventing garbage collection.

## Object_timeouts

All objects in STRVCT inherit timeout management through the `Object_timeouts` category on `Object`. This provides named, trackable timeouts that can be cancelled individually or in bulk — replacing direct `setTimeout` calls throughout the framework.

Direct `setTimeout` calls are fire-and-forget: there is no built-in way to cancel them by name, deduplicate them, or cancel all pending timers on an object at once. Worse, because the browser's timer queue holds a strong reference to the callback closure — which typically captures `this` — the target object cannot be garbage collected until every pending timer fires, even if nothing else references it. `Object_timeouts` solves both problems: named timeouts with automatic deduplication prevent timer accumulation, and the `addWeakTimeout` variant breaks the strong reference chain so that unreachable objects can be collected without waiting for their timers.

### Basic Usage

```javascript
// Fire after a delay
this.addTimeout(() => this.doSomething(), 1000);

// Named timeout (replaces any existing timeout with the same name)
this.addTimeout(() => this.poll(), 5000, "pollTimer");

// Cancel a named timeout
this.clearTimeoutNamed("pollTimer");

// Cancel all timeouts on this object
this.cancelAllTimeouts();
```

### Strong vs Weak Timeouts

The framework provides two timeout methods with different garbage collection behavior:

**`addTimeout(func, delay, name)`** — The standard timeout. The browser's timer queue holds a strong reference to the callback closure, which typically captures `this`. This **prevents the object from being garbage collected** until the timer fires. Use this when the work must happen regardless of the object's lifecycle — network retries, resource cleanup, message delivery guarantees.

**`addWeakTimeout(func, delay, name)`** — A GC-friendly timeout. Stores the callback on the object itself and uses only a `WeakRef` in the `setTimeout` closure. If the object becomes unreachable before the timer fires, it can be collected and the timer silently becomes a no-op. Use this for work that only matters while the object is alive — UI updates, animations, gesture state management.

```javascript
// Strong: retry must happen even if no one holds a reference to this request
this.addTimeout(() => this.retryRequest(), 5000);

// Weak: animation only matters if the view still exists
this.addWeakTimeout(() => this.fadeOut(), 300);
```

<svg viewBox="0 0 820 380" width="820" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <style>
    text { font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 12px; fill: #111; }
    .b { font-weight: 600; }
    .dim { fill: #666; }
    .box { fill: none; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .fill { fill: #f0ede5; stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; }
    .strong { stroke: #111; stroke-width: 1; fill: none; }
    .weak { stroke: #888; stroke-width: 1; stroke-dasharray: 4 3; fill: none; }
  </style>

    </marker>
  </defs>
