# Accessibility Testing & Tuning

Validating and refining the framework's ARIA implementation across screen readers, devices, and applications.

**Status:** ongoing; checked against the code 2026-11-23. **Built 2026-11-23:** the [navigation announcements](docs/Plans/Accessibility%20Testing%20%26%20Tuning/#navigation-announcement-mechanism), and the breadcrumb bar's `aria-current="location"` put back (it was lost when the bar became `SvBreadCrumbsView` on 2026-06-12). Both are checked in Chromium by `tests/e2e/navigation-announcements.spec.js` in the app repo, which reads the live region's text and attributes. **Not yet heard with a screen reader**: a pass with VoiceOver is the next check. What this plan waited on is done: [Browser Cleanup](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/) is built and its compaction coordinator released (2026-11-22). **Order:** the VoiceOver check of the announcements; the automated checks (last section), which do not exist yet in either repo; then the manual screen-reader passes, which no longer wait: the first [Tile Container Views](docs/Plans/Tile%20Container%20Views/) grid is built (2026-11-23), with the list role a list has.

## Overview

The core accessibility infrastructure is in place -- ARIA roles, labels, states, landmarks, live regions, focus indicators, and slot-to-ARIA metadata wiring are all implemented in the framework's view classes (see [Accessibility](docs/Accessibility/) documentation). What remains is testing that implementation against real assistive technology and tuning behavior for edge cases that only surface during actual screen reader use.

## VoiceOver Testing

macOS VoiceOver is the primary testing target since it's built into the development platform.

- Walk through a representative application with VoiceOver enabled (Cmd+F5)
- Verify that tile navigation announces tile content (`aria-label` from `title()`)
- Verify that field tiles announce their role, label, and current value
- Verify that boolean fields announce as checkboxes with checked state
- Verify that action fields announce as buttons with enabled/disabled state
- Verify that option lists announce as listbox with selected option
- Verify that breadcrumbs announce as navigation with current location
- Verify that `aria-live` regions announce new content (chat messages, status updates)
- Verify that landmark roles provide useful navigation shortcuts (VO+U landmarks menu)

## Tab Key / Screen Reader Interaction

The framework overrides native Tab behavior with a custom `nextKeyView` chain. This may conflict with screen reader conventions.

- Test whether VoiceOver's Tab navigation (VO+Tab) works correctly with `tabindex=-1` tiles
- Determine if the `nextKeyView` chain needs to be suspended when a screen reader is detected
- Investigate `aria-activedescendant` as an alternative to physical focus movement for tile navigation
- Verify that form fields within tiles receive focus correctly when Tab is pressed

## Navigation Announcement Mechanism

The policy: announce programmatic navigation, stay silent on user-initiated navigation.

**Built 2026-11-23.** Every move through `SvBrowserView.navigate(aRequest)` carries a cause, and a model's focus notes are now selected on behalf of a `"program"` request ([Browser Cleanup](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/#second-pass-built-2026-11-23)). When a browser's path changes, it asks the request behind the change (`SvNavigationRequest.isSpokenToScreenReader()`: true only for `"program"`) and, if so, says the new place's title through `SvLiveAnnouncer`. That is the page's one polite live region (`role="status"`), out of sight but in the accessibility tree. It empties itself and writes the title a moment later, so the same place said twice is heard twice, and a burst of moves is heard as its last.

- Spoken: the app's opening move, a model's `onRequestNavigateToNode`, a focus or focus-and-expand note (a new session opening its chat, a new item opened after an add).
- Not spoken: a tile, key or breadcrumb the user chose, an address typed or Back, a browser settling into its base state.
- **Left:** hear it with VoiceOver, on a Mac and on an iPhone. Check that a polite announcement is not cut off by the focus moving at the same moment, and that a session's opening (several moves in a row) says one useful thing rather than several.

## Cross-Screen-Reader Testing

Different screen readers have different behaviors and ARIA support levels.

- **NVDA on Windows** -- the most popular free screen reader; test with Firefox and Chrome
- **JAWS on Windows** -- the most widely used commercial screen reader
- **TalkBack on Android** -- test with Chrome on Android
- Verify that ARIA roles, states, and properties work consistently across readers
- Document any reader-specific workarounds needed

## Per-Application Adjustments

The framework provides good defaults, but some content needs application-level attention.

- **Alternative text for images** -- the framework can't infer what a picture shows; applications must provide `alt` text for meaningful images
- **Custom views** -- any view that overrides default rendering may need custom ARIA attributes
- **Domain-specific labels** -- where auto-generated slot descriptions aren't clear enough, applications should override `title()` or provide `aria-label` overrides
- **Complex widgets** -- application-specific composite widgets (e.g., dice rollers, map views) need manual ARIA patterns

## Color Contrast Verification

The default dark theme has been reviewed for WCAG 4.5:1 contrast compliance. Remaining work:

- Run automated contrast checks (axe, Lighthouse) against a running application
- Verify contrast ratios for all interactive states (hover, focus, disabled, selected)
- Check contrast in light theme variants if applicable
- Verify that `prefers-contrast: more` media query produces sufficient enhancement
- Ensure information is not conveyed by color alone -- use shape, text, or pattern as reinforcement

## Text Resize Testing

WCAG 1.4.4 requires content to be usable at 200% text size.

- Test with browser zoom at 200%
- Verify that content reflows correctly at 320px equivalent viewport width (WCAG 1.4.10)
- Check that no content is clipped or overlapping at increased text sizes
- Verify that STRVCT's flexbox-based layout accommodates text expansion gracefully

## Focus Management Refinements

- **Focus trapping in modals** -- when a modal dialog is open, Tab should cycle within the dialog
- **Focus restoration** -- drilling out should restore focus to the tile that was drilled into
- **Skip links** -- provide a way to skip past repetitive navigation to main content
- Verify that focus is visible and meets WCAG 2.2 contrast requirements (3:1 against adjacent colors) in all themes

## Automated Regression Testing

- Evaluate integrating axe-core or similar into the test suite for automated ARIA validation
- Consider adding Playwright accessibility assertions for critical navigation paths
- Set up CI checks that flag new accessibility regressions


---

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Async Final Initialization -->
Source: docs/Plans/Async%20Final%20Initialization/

# Async Final Initialization

Adding an async phase to the object initialization lifecycle.

**Status:** not planned (2026-11-13). Its main case, stubs that need data before they can display, was solved first by manifest metadata and then by [Lazy Slots](docs/Plans/Lazy%20Slots/), which load synchronously. Reopen it if a second real case appears that neither covers. The page is kept for the analysis.

## Context

When objects need async data during initialization (e.g., fetching from cloud storage, API calls), the current synchronous initialization flow (`init()` → `finalInit()` → `afterInit()`) doesn't accommodate this cleanly.

## The Idea

Add an `asyncFinalInit()` phase that runs after synchronous initialization but before the object is considered "fully ready."

## Potential Benefits

- Clean architectural pattern — async initialization gets its own explicit phase
- Objects have a clear "fully ready" state
- Generalizes to many async initialization scenarios
- Could handle lazy-loaded cloud data, API-dependent initialization, etc.

## Challenges to Solve

### Initialization State Tracking

- Objects need an `isFullyInitialized` flag
- Anything accessing them needs to check or wait for completion
- Views need to handle "initializing" state gracefully (loading indicators, disabled interactions)

### Cascading Dependencies

- If object A's `asyncFinalInit` depends on object B's `asyncFinalInit`, ordering becomes complex
- Need dependency resolution or explicit waiting mechanisms
- Risk of deadlocks if dependencies are circular

### Validation Timing

- Current validation runs synchronously and may depend on async data
- Options to consider:
  - Defer all validation until after `asyncFinalInit`
  - Add a `validationReady` state that skips validation when false
  - Make validation itself async-aware
- Example: Options dropdown validation needs character names, but characters are lazy-loaded stubs

### Persistence Edge Cases

- What happens if object is accessed/modified before `asyncFinalInit` completes?
- Should writes be queued? Rejected? Merged later?
- How does this interact with the dirty tracking system?

### UI Synchronization

- Views may render before async data is ready
- Need consistent pattern for showing loading states
- Re-render triggers when `asyncFinalInit` completes

## Alternative Approaches Considered

**Manifest-Based Metadata:** For the specific case of lazy-loaded cloud objects, storing display metadata (title, subtitle) in a manifest allows stubs to display correctly without fetching full data. The data is synchronously available — just stored in a different place.

- Pros: No framework changes, uses existing infrastructure
- Cons: Only works when you control what metadata goes in the manifest

**Async Closures for Options:** Add `validItemsAsyncClosure` to slots/options that returns a Promise. The options node shows "Loading..." until the closure resolves.

- Pros: Localized to options, doesn't affect whole initialization flow
- Cons: Adds complexity to Slot and SvOptionsNode, may be over-engineering for limited use cases
- Note: This was implemented and then removed in favor of the manifest approach

## Open Questions

- How common is async initialization across the codebase? Is framework support warranted?
- Should `asyncFinalInit` be opt-in per class, or a universal phase?
- How would this interact with the persistence system's `loadFromRecord` flow?
- Could a simpler "initialization complete" event/notification pattern suffice?

## Related Patterns in Other Frameworks

- React's `useEffect` for async operations after render
- SwiftUI's `.task` modifier for async work tied to view lifecycle
- Android's `ViewModel` with `init` blocks and coroutine scopes


---

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Async Navigation -->
Source: docs/Plans/Async%20Navigation/

# Async Navigation

Rearchitecting the navigation stack to support asynchronous loading at every level.

## Status

**Direction, no work planned** (2026-11-13). Windowed collections (`setSubnodesAreWindowed`, `loadLatestWindow`, `loadOlderWindow`) and synchronous [lazy slots](docs/Plans/Lazy%20Slots/) have since met the large-collection and cold-data cases with the navigation stack still synchronous. This is a long-term architectural direction, not expected to happen soon. The current synchronous navigation model works well for the common case and is significantly simpler to reason about. This page captures the motivation and tradeoffs for future reference.

## Context

STRVCT's navigation stack is currently synchronous. When a user drills into a node, its subnodes are expected to be available immediately in memory -- the tile container reads the subnode array, creates tiles, and displays them in the same frame. This synchronous guarantee makes the navigation code straightforward: there are no loading states, no cancellation of in-flight requests, no partial renders, and no race conditions between navigation events.

However, this model assumes all data is local. As the framework is used with cloud-backed data, server-side collections, or very large hierarchies, the assumption that subnodes are always available breaks down. Async navigation would allow any level of the hierarchy to load its children on demand -- from a remote API, a lazy database query, or any other asynchronous source.

## What Would Change

The synchronous contract runs deep through the navigation stack:

- **`SvStackView`** assumes column content is ready when a navigation event fires.
- **`SvNavView`** assumes it can read a node's subnodes and build tiles immediately.
- **`SvTilesView`** assumes the subnode array is complete and in memory.
- **Tile creation** assumes the node it represents is fully initialized.

An async-capable navigation stack would need to handle the possibility that any of these steps returns a promise rather than a value. This means:

- **Loading states**: Each navigation level needs a placeholder (spinner, skeleton tiles, or empty state) while data loads.
- **Cancellation**: If the user navigates away before loading completes, in-flight requests must be cancelled to avoid stale data arriving in the wrong column.
- **Error handling**: Network failures, timeouts, and partial results need UI treatment at every level, not just at the data layer.
- **Progressive rendering**: Results may arrive incrementally -- the container needs to render partial subnode sets and update as more arrive.
- **Back-navigation caching**: Previously loaded levels should be cached so drilling out doesn't re-fetch.

## Performance Tradeoffs

The synchronous model is fast precisely because it avoids async overhead. Making navigation async introduces significant performance costs even when data is local:

- **Microtask overhead**: Every `await` yields to the microtask queue, adding latency between navigation steps. A drill-in that currently takes one synchronous frame would span multiple frames even if all data is cached, creating visible delay or flicker.
- **Layout thrashing**: Progressive rendering (show spinner, then replace with content) causes multiple layout passes. The current model lays out tiles once.
- **Complexity tax**: Every call site in the navigation chain gains error handling, cancellation logic, and state management. This isn't just code complexity -- it's runtime cost from additional branching, promise allocation, and state tracking on every navigation event.
- **Synchronous fast path**: Even with an async architecture, the common case (local data) should remain fast. Maintaining a synchronous fast path alongside async support adds implementation complexity and testing surface.
- **Memory pressure**: Caching previously loaded levels for back-navigation trades memory for responsiveness. The cache eviction policy itself becomes a source of bugs and tuning.

These tradeoffs are the primary reason this is a long-term direction rather than an immediate goal. The current synchronous model is the right default for most applications -- the performance cost of async navigation is only worth paying when the data genuinely can't be local.

## Relationship to Other Work

Several other plans intersect with async navigation:

- **[Lazy Slots](docs/Plans/Lazy%20Slots/)** and **[Promise-Wrapped Slots](docs/Plans/Promise-Wrapped%20Slots/)** address async data at the slot level. Async navigation would be the view-layer counterpart -- the container knowing how to wait for and display async subnode sources.
- **[Scaling to Large Collections](docs/Plans/Tile%20Container%20Views/)** (in Tile Container Views) describes virtual scrolling and async data sources for tile containers. Async navigation generalizes this from a single container feature to a stack-wide capability.
- **[Graph Database](docs/Plans/Graph%20Database/)** would introduce query-based node retrieval, which naturally produces async results.

Lazy slots were implemented, but synchronously: a pool's records are in memory once it opens, so loading an object needs no await. What remains genuinely async is opening another pool (`asyncResolveFar`) and fetching from a server, and that is where this direction would start if it is ever needed.


---

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Browser Cleanup -->
Source: docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/

# Browser Cleanup

Simplifying and documenting the browser navigation architecture.

**Status:** built: parts 1 to 4, and part 1's second pass (checked against the code 2026-11-23). (1) One navigation entry point: built 2026-11-19, see [below](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/#one-navigation-entry-point). (2) The compaction coordinator: released 2026-11-22, see [Compaction Coordinator](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/). (3) Composable breadcrumbs and (4) the auxiliary view were built on 2026-06-12, before this plan was last revised, which did not notice: each browser owns its own `SvBreadCrumbsView`, and a node's `nodeCompanionNode()` gives it a [companion](docs/Views/Companion%20View/) with an embedded browser of its own. The entry point's [second pass](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/#second-pass-built-2026-11-23) was built on 2026-11-23, with the navigation announcements in [Accessibility Testing & Tuning](docs/Plans/Accessibility%20Testing%20%26%20Tuning/). **Left:** the parts of the auxiliary-view sketch the companion did not take, which wait for a node that uses a companion ([below](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/#auxiliary-view)). The compaction notes from Cleanup Notes are merged in below.

## Current Architecture

The browser is built from four cooperating classes that implement a recursive Miller column navigation pattern:

### SvBrowserView

The top-level container. An `SvNodeView` (since 2026-06-12; before that a subclass of `SvStackView`) that owns two subviews: an `SvBreadCrumbsView` above an `SvStackView` rooted at the browser's node. It is the one way in for navigation (`navigate(aRequest)`), listens for `onRequestNavigateToNode` / `onRequestSelectNodePath` when `handlesGlobalNavRequests` is set (an embedded browser clears it), handles keyboard shortcuts, and settles into its base state when nobody has navigated it.

### SvStackView

The core navigation primitive. Each stack view is a pair: a **nav view** on the left (or top) showing the selected node's subnodes as selectable tiles, and an **other view** on the right (or bottom) that contains the next `SvStackView` for deeper navigation. This recursive nesting is what produces the Miller column layout.

Key responsibilities:

- **Path selection**: `selectNodePathArray(pathArray)` walks an array of nodes, selecting one at each level and recursing into the next stack view.
- **Path reporting**: `selectedNodePathArray()` and `selectedPathTitlesString()` return the current selection path by walking up or down the stack chain.
- **Direction**: The `direction` slot (`"right"` or `"down"`) controls whether subnodes lay out as side-by-side columns or stacked rows. Nodes set this via `setNodeIsVertical()` -- the stack view reads it and adjusts its flex direction accordingly. The recursive combination of different directions at each level is what distinguishes STRVCT's navigation from a standard Miller column browser.
- **Compaction**: each level states a claim (`layerClaim()`); the root runs one allocation over the chain (`SvLayerAllocation`) when a claim, the chain or a width has changed, and each column applies its answer (`applyLayerAnswer()`). See [Compaction Coordinator](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/).
- **Notification broadcasting**: When the user selects a tile, the path change bubbles up the view parents (`childUpdatedNavPath`) to the first `SvBrowserView`, which updates its own breadcrumbs, posts a sender-scoped `onBrowserViewPathChange`, and stops it there, so navigation inside an embedded browser never reaches an outer one. The older global `onStackViewPathChange` note still posts.

### SvNavView

An individual navigation column within a stack view. Contains a header, a scrollable tile container (`SvTilesView`), and a footer. When assigned a node via `setNode()`, it populates the tiles view with that node's subnodes.

Additional features:

- **Gesture-based resizing**: Users can drag the right or bottom edge to resize the column. The new size is stored on the node (`nodeMinTileWidth` / `nodeMinTileHeight`), so it persists across navigation.
- **Collapse / uncollapse**: The compaction system can hide a nav view entirely when space is tight, replacing it with a back-navigation affordance.
- **Orientation sync**: Reads the parent stack view's direction and adjusts its own layout accordingly.

### SvBreadCrumbsView

The breadcrumb bar: a back button and one clickable segment per node in its browser's path. A plain view owned by the browser, with no node (it was a tile in the model graph, `SvBreadCrumbsTile`, until 2026-06-12). Its browser tells it when the path changes, so it reflects only navigation beneath that browser, and each browser on screen has its own. A click hands its browser a request with the cause `"user"`.

The breadcrumbs also compact: when the path is too long to fit, earlier crumbs are hidden and a back arrow appears that navigates to the most recent hidden crumb.

## Navigation Flow

When the user clicks a tile:

1. `SvTilesView` selects the tile and notifies its `SvNavView`.
2. The nav view's parent `SvStackView` calls `didChangeNavSelection()`.
3. This propagates up the view parents to the first `SvBrowserView`, which records the path change and posts `onBrowserViewPathChange`.
4. That browser's `SvBreadCrumbsView` rebuilds its segments.
5. The next `SvStackView` in the chain receives the selected node and populates its nav view.

When the user clicks a breadcrumb:

1. The breadcrumb bar reads the stored path array from the clicked button.
2. It hands the browser a request: `browser.navigate(SvNavigationRequest.toPath(path).setCause("user"))`.
3. The stack chain recursively selects each node in the path, collapsing deeper levels.
4. The resulting path change reaches the browser as in the steps above, and the breadcrumbs update.

## Cleanup Opportunities

The browser navigation works well but has accumulated complexity over time. Areas to consider:

### Clearer separation of concerns

`SvStackView` handles direction, compaction, path selection, and notification broadcasting. Some of these could be factored into smaller, more focused collaborators -- for example, a compaction manager or a path selection coordinator.

### Compaction logic

**Released 2026-11-22** (app PR #788). The plan and what was built are in [Compaction Coordinator](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/). What this section asked for, and where it stands:

- **A compaction coordinator.** Built as claims stated by the views and one function, `SvLayerAllocation`, that allocates over the whole chain with no DOM. `TestLayerAllocation` holds its rules.
- **A written protocol.** The plan's [What asks for a pass](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#what-asks-for-a-pass) and the function's tests are the protocol. A pass runs only when a claim, the chain or a width has changed.
- **Measure once.** Done: a streamed response that ran 204 to 264 passes before runs none.
- **Priorities** (an order of giving way other than from the left) and **animation** are not built. Priorities are a part D item in the coordinator's plan, taken up when a case needs one.

### One navigation entry point

**Built 2026-11-19.** `selectNodePathArray()`, `navigateToNode()`, `selectNodePathString()`, `selectPathWithRetry()` and `moveToBase()` all navigated, through different code, and none said who asked. Now there is one way in:

```javascript
browser.navigate(SvNavigationRequest.toPath([a, b]).setCause("user"));
```

An `SvNavigationRequest` says where and who.

| Where | Made with |
| --- | --- |
| A path of nodes (a leading browser root is skipped) | `toPath(nodes)` |
| A node, by its parent chain | `toNode(aNode)` |
| A slash-separated title path, as a URL holds it | `toPathString("A/B")` |
| The browser's base state | `toBaseState()` |

| Cause | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `"user"` | The user's own act: a tile, a breadcrumb, a link in the content, a tab tapped again. |
| `"url"` | The address changed, or the page was opened at one. |
| `"program"` | Code moved the user without their asking for that place (the default). |
| `"base"` | A browser nobody has navigated settling into its base state. |

What it does and what it replaced:

- **One mechanism.** Every request gets the bounded retry while columns materialize and announces its arrival as a tap does. Before, only some routes retried, and a URL into a column that wasn't built yet was lost.
- **Who asked is remembered.** `browser.lastNavigationRequest()` is the request behind the latest path change. A listener to `onBrowserViewPathChange` asks it for the cause; this is what the navigation announcements in Accessibility Testing & Tuning need.
- **Model code is unchanged.** A model never references a view, so it still posts `onRequestNavigateToNode` or `onRequestSelectNodePath`. The browser turns each into a request with the cause `"program"`.
- **Panes.** An anchored-tabs stack hands the rest of a path to its pane with `continuingRequestToPath()`, so the pane's request carries the cause of the whole navigation.
- **Removed.** `navigateToNode`, `selectNodePathString`, `selectPathWithRetry` and the unused `setSelectedPathTitlesArray` / `setSelectedPathTitlesString`. The stack's `selectNodePathArray()` stays as the walk itself, called only by the browser.
- **Kept from sliding back.** `TestNavigationEntryPoint` fails when anything but the browser calls the stack's walk, or when a retired method returns. `tests/e2e/navigation-entry-point.spec.js` (in the app repo) checks each route and its cause in a browser.

Three decisions (Steve, 2026-11-19):

1. **A request object, not arguments.** New needs (which stack view, don't take focus) become slots, and call sites don't change.
2. **A tile the user taps reports afterwards.** The columns select it as before; the browser hears of the path change and records a request whose cause is the user. Nothing can veto or redirect a tap before it happens. That moves through the entry point with the compaction coordinator (part 2), the first thing that needs it.
3. **Focus-and-expand waits for a second pass.** `postShouldFocusAndExpandSubnode` and `postShouldFocusSubnode` ("show this child of where I am", about 16 call sites, most of them in the app) still select in the columns directly, so the path change they cause is recorded as the user's. Until the second pass, an announcement keyed on the cause will miss them.

#### Second pass (built 2026-11-23)

- **The focus notes are code's moves.** `postShouldFocusSubnode` and `postShouldFocusAndExpandSubnode` are still carried out by the column that shows the parent: it scrolls to the tile and opens it, which a path walk from the root would not do. That column now does it on behalf of a request with the cause `"program"` (`SvTilesView.selectForModel()` → `SvBrowserView.selectInColumnsFor()`), so the path change is recorded as code's and not the user's. A navigation already under way keeps its own cause. This differs from the first plan, which was to send the notes through `navigate()`; the column keeps its own scrolling and opening, and the browser hears who asked.
- **Every note is code's**, including one posted after the user's own add. The user asked for the new item, but not for the browser to move to it, so a screen reader should hear where they are.
- **Left as the user's, on purpose:** a column folding because its node was removed (`nodeBecameOrphan`), and a selected tile rebinding to a new instance. Neither takes the user anywhere new, and both stay silent.
- **Checked** by `TestNavigationEntryPoint` (both notes go through the request; nothing is left pending, even when the selection throws) and, in a browser against `just launch`, by `tests/e2e/navigation-announcements.spec.js` in the app repo. `navigation-entry-point.spec.js` and `meta-plan-step-a.spec.js` still pass.

### Mobile and responsive behavior

The compaction system provides basic responsive behavior, but a dedicated mobile navigation mode (e.g., single-column with swipe gestures) could replace the current approach of compacting columns until they fit.

### Composable breadcrumbs

**Built 2026-06-12.** The breadcrumbs used to be a node in the tree (`SvBreadCrumbsTile`) that found its target by walking up to the root stack view, so a browser could have only one set. Now each `SvBrowserView` owns an `SvBreadCrumbsView`, and a path change bubbles only to the nearest browser. An embedded browser, such as the one inside a companion, has its own trail and its own path, independent of the main one.

### Auxiliary view

**Built 2026-06-12, as the companion.** A node answers `nodeCompanionNode()` with another node, and `SvDetailView` shows that node beside (or below) the node's navigation in an `SvCompanionView` holding an embedded browser, with its own breadcrumbs, selection and compaction. It is docked, collapsed to a tab behind an edge handle, or hidden when there is no room; the user's dock or tab choice is kept, and Cmd+\\ toggles the deepest one. See [Companion View](docs/Views/Companion%20View/). In the compaction pass, companions are sized before the columns, which then compact around the reservation.

The sketch that stood here proposed five hints. The companion took one and left the view to decide the rest:

| Sketched | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `setNodeAuxiliaryNode(node)` | `nodeCompanionNode()` |
| `setNodeAuxiliaryPosition("right" / "bottom")` | Not a hint; the edge follows the stack's direction (right, or bottom for a `"down"` stack). |
| `setNodeAuxiliaryDefaultState("expanded" / "collapsed")` | Not a hint; chosen from the space it is offered until the user pins docked or tab. |
| `setNodeAuxiliaryCompactsFirst(true)` | Not a hint; the columns compact around a docked companion, and a window too narrow for it hides it whatever the pin. |
| `setNodeAuxiliaryMaxColumns(n)` | Not built; the embedded browser compacts within its own width. |

**No node in the framework or the app supplies a companion yet**, so none of this has been seen in use. The companion's code is kept and nothing is spent on it until one does (Compaction Coordinator, decision 17); the missing hints wait for that node too.


---

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Capabilities & Permissions -->
Source: docs/Plans/Capabilities%20%26%20Permissions/

# Capabilities & Permissions

Asking "can this caller do this here?" in one place, answered by the pool's store, so that views offer only what will be honored and a refused write is never silent.

**Status:** built, and seen working in a browser on 2026-11-19, through the model against `just launch` and through the views on the deployed dev project ([Meta Plan](docs/Plans/Meta%20Plan/#done-the-2026-11-18-steps), step A). That pass found and fixed one more edit path that did not ask the cascade (Cmd+D and pinch-to-add). Rewritten 2026-11-13 to build on the editability cascade and the Record Store, which both shipped after the first draft. The editing half is in use (`SvNode_editability`); the questions about reading, sharing and authority, and the denial path, are not. Step 1 is done (2026-11-16): every edit path in the view layer asks the cascade, and a test keeps it so. The rest was agreed and built 2026-11-17 as [the design questions](docs/Plans/Capabilities%20%26%20Permissions/#design-questions-for-steps-2-to-4) settle it: the server says who may write, the pool's answer is the cascade's default, and a refused commit reloads and says so. Checked headless, with the server's contract tests on the Firestore backing, and in a browser against `just launch` (a forced save refused 403, reloaded and said; `editability-browser-pass.spec.js`); not yet on the Spanner backing.

## Context

A concrete failure in one application: a non-admin user dragged a JSON file onto an admin-only catalog. The local model accepted the change, the dirty flag fired, a save animation ran, and the write was dropped at the sync layer. The user found out on the next reload. Two layers needed a gate, and each reimplemented the same admin check.

Two things have shipped since:

- **The editability cascade.** `subtreeIsUserEditable` is a tri-state slot (null means "ask the parent"); `effectiveUserEditability()` walks up the parent and owner chain, and views ask `offersUserEdit(rawCapability)` before offering an edit, a delete, an add or a pick. It is deliberately a UI affordance, not authority: server rules remain the write gate. Since 2026-11-16 every edit path in the view layer consults it (step 1 below).
- **The Record Store.** A pool is one document, and it is the unit of sync and of permission: a far reference "keeps nothing alive and grants no permissions", and resolving it opens the target pool under the target's own permissions.

## Proposed Shape

### 1. Close the editing gaps — done (2026-11-16)

Every edit path in the view layer now asks the cascade, which fixes the catalog failure on the UI side. Before, field values, add and delete asked; these did not:

- **Titles and subtitles** (`SvTitledTile`, `SvActionFieldTile`).
- **Dragging a node in, and reordering** (`SvTilesView.acceptsDropHover()`, `SvTile.acceptsDropHoverComplete()`, `canReorderTiles()`).
- **Dragging a node out.** A move removes the node from its list, so from a read-only list a drag is a copy.
- **Dropping a file from the desktop** (`SvTilesView.onBrowserDropChunk()`). It is refused with a message rather than silently: the node's `noteUserEditRefused()` posts `onRequestUserAlert`, "You can't edit 'Monster Catalog'." The app's own catalog drop gate, which did this for two classes, is gone.
- **Field paths the first audit missed:** the option picker's toggle, the video well, the chat input.

`tests/headless/TestEditabilityCascade.js` checks the cascade's answers and the refusal message. `tests/headless/TestEditabilityInViews.js` scans the view layer for a raw capability read (`nodeCanEditTitle()`, `canDelete()`, `valueIsEditable()`, `acceptsAddingSubnode()`, …) without `offersUserEdit()`; run over the code before this step it finds all 11 sites. Checked headless only.

### 2. The pool answers for its contents

`effectiveUserEditability()` today ends the walk with `true`. Instead, a node whose chain has no opinion asks the pool it lives in, and the pool asks its store:

- `SvRecordStoreProtocol` gains an optional `callerRolesForPool(poolId)` (or `callerCanWrite(poolId)`), answered synchronously from what the store already knows: the local store says "all", the cloud store says what the pool's membership and the server rules allow.
- An optional method with a default, not a new protocol: the shape [Complete Protocols](docs/Plans/Complete%20Protocols/) settled on for hooks most implementers don't need.
- The answer is cached on the pool and refreshed when membership changes, so a tile pass doesn't cost a lookup per node.

This keeps one answer for the view and for the store: the store that will refuse the write is the one that told the view not to offer it.

### 3. More than editing

The cascade answers one question. The others, as optional hooks on `SvNode` with defaults, consulted the same way:

- `callerCanRead()` — default true. For hidden or partly shared content.
- `callerCanDelete()` — default: what editing says.
- `callerCanShare()` — default false.
- `callerCanCreate(aClass)` — default: what editing says. Lets a node accept edits while limiting which children may be added.

Each resolves through the cascade and then the pool, as in 2.

### 4. Refusals are never silent

When the store refuses a write anyway (stale cache, a rule the client didn't know), it posts a domain notification naming the node and the action, and the UI shows it through the existing user-alert path (`onRequestUserAlert`). The message names the thing, not the role: "You can't edit 'Monster Catalog'." The local change is rolled back with `pool.transaction()` where it ran in one.

## Why This Shape

- **One gate per question.** Views and the store ask the same thing and get the same answer.
- **Role names stay out of call sites.** "Admin" becoming "catalog editor" and "catalog publisher" changes the store's policy, not the views.
- **Per-node policy is an override.** Draft/published, locked during a long operation, read-only after archive: each is a node overriding a hook, not a new flag.

## Design Questions for Steps 2 to 4

**Agreed and built 2026-11-17.** Each answer is given with its reasoning; [What Was Built](docs/Plans/Capabilities%20%26%20Permissions/#what-was-built) lists where it differs. Where one changes a step above, it says so.

What the code did before, which these were built on:

- The client decides "may this person edit the catalog?" from the `role: "admin"` claim in the sign-in token (`UoModel.callerIsAdmin()`). The server decides from the caller's row in the scope's `_members` (`assertCanWrite`: owner or editor). The server's own notes call membership "the enforced definition" and the claim "a separate auth-side concern". The two can disagree in both directions.
- The server already looks the caller's role up on every read (`assertCanRead`), and does not send it back.
- A pool does not know its scope. The scope is on the pool's root row on the server; the app passes it as a commit option.
- The client threw the server's error code away. The server replies `403` with `code: "permission-denied"` in the body; the request layer kept only the number, so `SvCloudRecordStore`'s test for a refusal never matched in production and a refused commit was thrown as an unknown failure. (`UoSessions` matched the message text to work around it.) `UoFsBackend.errorCodeNameFor()` now passes the code on.
- A refused commit comes back as `{ status: "refused", reason }` for four different causes (permission, invalid argument, failed precondition, not signed in). `UoCloudDocument` rethrows all four as one error, nothing tells the user, and the local edit stays dirty and is retried on every sync pass.
- A conflict, by contrast, has a finished path: reload from the cloud, check whether the reload lost anything the refused commit carried, and tell the user only if it did (`handleWriteConflict`).
- A guest's session is a replica: a pool the guest can never commit, in which the guest still types, picks and rolls. Those travel to the host as messages.

### Q1. Where does the answer come from, and what about the admin claim?

**Recommendation: the server answers, with every pool read, and the client stops consulting the admin claim for editing.**

- The read functions add `callerCanWrite` (a boolean) to what they return for a pool. The lookup is already done, so it costs nothing, and the answer can't be older than the data it arrives with.
- A boolean, not the role name. "Owner or editor may write" is the server's rule; if it becomes "catalog publisher", no client code changes. A role name on the client is the same mistake as the admin check, one level down. If a view later needs "owner" for sharing, that is its own question (Q4).
- The cloud store keeps the answer per pool; the pool asks its store. `SvRecordStoreProtocol` gains an optional `callerCanWritePool(poolId)` whose default is true, which is what the local and memory stores say.
- `UoGenres.subtreeIsUserEditable()` and `UoPublicCatalogCollection.callerCanEdit()` then read that answer and the admin check behind them goes. The claim keeps its real job, gating the admin site and `bootstrapRoot`.

Why not make admins editors and keep the client check: `grantCatalogAdmin` already does make them owners, so today the two usually agree. But "usually" is the problem: two rules that agree by convention drift, and the failure when they drift is the silent loss this plan exists to end. One rule, asked of the party that enforces it, cannot drift.

**Before the answer is known.** A pool made on this device, or in the caller's own scope, is writable: no server is needed to know that. A pool opened from the local mirror before the cloud has been reached uses the last answer, kept with the mirror, so an offline start looks like the last session. Otherwise not offered until the read lands, which is the same moment the content does.

### Q2. How does the store's answer combine with the cascade?

**Recommendation: the pool's answer replaces the cascade's final `true`. The nearest node opinion still wins, in both directions.** This changes what I first proposed (the store's answer always wins).

"The store only ever restricts" is the obvious rule and it breaks sessions. A guest's replica pool is unwritable by design, so the rule would turn off the guest's chat input, option picks and dice, all of which are legitimate: they are not edits of the pool, they are messages to the host. Since step 1 the chat input asks the cascade (rightly: a non-editor should not drive a catalog campaign's assistant), so this is not hypothetical.

So the question the cascade answers stays "should an edit be offered here?", and the pool supplies the default for everything under it:

- No opinion anywhere in the chain: the pool's answer. This covers the catalog with no app code.
- A node says `false`: read-only, whatever the pool says (a session's party).
- A node says `true`: offered, whatever the pool says. It is a statement that input here does not travel through this pool's commit. The guest's session surface declares it once.

The risk is someone setting `true` to quiet a read-only complaint and bringing the silent loss back. Q3 is the backstop: a refused write is announced, so the mistake is loud the first time it runs.

This also settles the last open question in the first draft: `subtreeIsUserEditable` and the pool's answer are different facts and both stay. The pool says whether the store will take a write; a node opinion says what the app means here.

### Q3. What happens to an edit the server refuses anyway?

**Recommendation: reload the document and tell the user, by the path conflicts already use. Only for a permission refusal.**

First, the four causes need to stop being one. The store passes the code through (`{ status: "refused", code, reason }`), and each gets what it needs:

| Refusal | What it means | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `permission-denied` | The caller may not write here | Reload from the cloud; tell the user if something was lost; the pool's answer becomes false, so the views go read-only |
| `unauthenticated` | The sign-in lapsed | Keep the edits; ask the user to sign in; the next save sends them |
| `invalid-argument`, `failed-precondition` | A bug: the client sent something malformed | Keep the edits; report the error; do not reload |

Dropping edits over a lapsed sign-in or over our own bug would be data loss we caused. Only the permission case has no future in which the edit can be saved.

For that case, reload rather than keep-and-mark:

- An edit that can never be saved is not a draft, it is a fork. It stays dirty, is retried every pass (the "403 storm" `UoSessions.onChildCloudSaveFailed` was written to stop), and shows this user a document nobody else sees.
- The machinery exists and has been exercised: `handleWriteConflict` reloads and asks `holdsCommitContent()` whether anything was lost. Usually a refused commit carries only defaults filled on load, and then nothing need be said.
- The message is `noteUserEditRefused()`'s, extended: "You can't edit 'Monster Catalog'. Your change wasn't kept."

The first draft said to roll back with `pool.transaction()`. That cannot work: the commit runs later and asynchronously, long after the edit's transaction closed.

Two details. The refused commit's content goes to the error report, so support can recover a real loss. And `UoSessions`' test of the message text (`/not an editor/`) to spot a deleted scope becomes a test of the code.

Each refusal is also a measurement: it means a view offered something it should not have. Reported, they are the list of gaps left in Q1 and Q2.

### Q4. Read, delete, share, create (step 3 above)

**Recommendation: not now. Add each one when a view offers something the server refuses.**

- Nothing calls them, and four hooks with defaults are four places to be subtly wrong with no test that matters.
- Reading needs no client gate: the server does not send what the caller may not read.
- Delete and create follow editing today, on client and server alike.
- Sharing is the one with a real separate rule (an invite needs the scope's owner). When the invite action is next touched it gets `callerCanShare`, answered the same way as Q1.

Q3's refusal reports say when this is wrong: a refusal for an action that editing allowed is the signal to add its hook.

### Q5. Roles that change mid-session

**Recommendation: no push. The answer refreshes on every read of the pool, on a refusal, and when an invite is accepted.**

Roles change rarely, and the cost of a stale answer is bounded by Q3: one refused edit, a clear message, and the answer corrected by the refusal itself. A live channel for membership is more moving parts than that cost justifies. When the answer changes, the pool tells its root, which re-syncs its views.

### Hide or disable?

**Recommendation: no new convention; keep what step 1 does.** Content stays where it is and renders read-only (a title that can't be edited, a field with no caret). A control whose only purpose is the edit is not shown (the add button, the delete swipe). A layout that reflows by permission would make the same document look different to an editor and a reader for no gain.

### What Was Built

In the order suggested: Q3, then Q1, then Q2. Q4 and Q5 need no work until something calls for them.

- **Q3.** `SvCloudRecordStore.asyncCommit()` answers `{ status: "refused", code, reason }`, and the pool adds the commit it sent. `UoCloudDocument.handleRefusedCommit()` does what the table says; a permission refusal reloads by the conflict path and tells the user once (`noteUserEditRefused("Your change wasn't kept.")`), with the commit's content in the error report. Every refusal is still thrown, with its code, so a folder can reconcile it. App test: `TestRefusedCommit.js`.
- **Q1.** The server's `openPool`, `readChanges` and the scope listing return `callerCanWrite`, from one rule (`roleMayWrite`) that `assertCanWrite` also uses; both backings, with a contract test. `SvCloudRecordStore` remembers the answer per pool and per scope (`callerCanWritePool()`, `callerCanWriteScope()`), and a commit taken or refused for permission updates it. Framework test: `TestCloudWriteAnswers.js`.
- **Q2.** `SvObjectPool.callerCanWrite` holds the answer, set when a document's pool is opened from the cloud or commits. `effectiveUserEditability()` makes a pool's root read-only when it is false. `UoClientSession` says `true`. `TestEditabilityCascade.js` covers it.

Where it differs from the answers above:

- **A store's "yes" is no opinion.** Only its "no" enters the cascade. Otherwise a writable document inside a deliberately read-only place (a session's party) would become editable again.
- **No protocol method.** Only the cloud store has an answer and only the app's documents ask it, so `SvRecordStoreProtocol` is unchanged. Add `callerCanWritePool()` to it when a second store has something to say.
- **The answer is not kept with the local mirror.** A document opened offline, before any read, is offered for editing until the first read says otherwise. Q3 covers the gap: a refused edit is announced and the document goes read-only.
- **The admin claim remains as the guess before the server has said.** `UoModel.callerCanWriteToScopeRoot()` asks the store; until the catalog's first listing answers (or against a server that does not say), the catalog goes by the claim as before. That also makes the client safe to ship before the server.


---

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Case Studies -->
Source: docs/Plans/Case%20Studies/

# Case Studies

Comparative implementations of small applications in STRVCT and conventional stacks.

**Status:** not started. **Order:** Contacts first, and early: it needs nothing the framework lacks, and what it turns up feeds the [Meta Plan](docs/Plans/Meta%20Plan/). The others once their features exist: Photo Gallery after the grid container, Discussion Forum after [Capabilities & Permissions](docs/Plans/Capabilities%20%26%20Permissions/), Knowledge Base and Bookmark Manager after search.

## Purpose

The naked objects pattern makes strong claims about development efficiency: the framework generates views from models, so developers write less code, and cross-cutting concerns like accessibility and persistence come automatically. These claims are testable.

Each case study would implement the same application in STRVCT and in a conventional React stack (React + React Router + a state library + a component library), built by LLMs under identical conditions. The comparison would measure:

- **Development effort** -- rounds of prompting, debugging iterations, total token usage
- **Code volume** -- lines of code, number of files, boilerplate ratio
- **Correctness** -- bugs found in manual testing, edge cases handled or missed
- **Accessibility** -- ARIA coverage without explicit effort, screen reader usability
- **Persistence and sync** -- how much code is required for local storage and cross-device sync
- **Time to feature** -- how quickly a new feature can be added to the existing app

Multiple LLMs could run the same studies independently to control for model-specific strengths.

## Core Requirements

Every case study app must meet these baseline requirements, because they represent what users expect from a real, useful application:

- **Local persistence** -- data survives page refresh and browser restart
- **Cloud sync** -- data is available across devices via authenticated user accounts
- **Accessibility** -- correct ARIA roles, labels, and states on all interactive elements; keyboard-navigable
- **Drag-to-reorder** -- lists that have a user-meaningful order support drag reordering

These features are often omitted from small apps not because users don't want them, but because the tools make them expensive to implement. A fair comparison should include them precisely because they reveal where framework design choices reduce or increase the cost of building what users actually need.

## Candidate Applications

Each app is small enough to build in a single session but non-trivial enough to exercise real framework features: persistence, cloud sync, navigation, editing, validation, and multiple data types.

### 1. Contacts

A personal contacts manager. Each contact has structured fields (name, phone numbers, email addresses, physical address, birthday, notes) with the ability to add multiple entries per field type. Contacts are grouped, searchable, and persisted with cross-device sync. Exercises: nested data structures, multiple field types, search/filtering, persistence, list navigation.

### 2. Photo Gallery

A personal photo gallery with albums containing images. Users upload images (with drag-and-drop), which are stored as blobs with generated thumbnails. Each image has a caption, tags, and date taken. Albums display as a grid of thumbnails; selecting an image opens a detail view. Images are drag-reorderable within albums. Supports bulk upload. Exercises: binary blob storage and retrieval, image upload and thumbnail generation, grid layout, lazy loading, media-heavy UI, drag-to-reorder in a grid context, tagging and filtering.

### 3. Project Tracker

A lightweight project management tool with projects containing tasks. Each task has a title, description, status (todo/in-progress/done), priority, due date, and assignee. Tasks can be drag-reordered within status groups. Exercises: enum fields (status, priority), date handling, drag-to-reorder, grouping/filtering by property, multiple navigation levels (project → task list → task detail).

### 4. Discussion Forum

A multi-user discussion forum with boards, threads, and posts. Users create accounts, post in threads, and see content from other users in real time. Thread authors can edit or delete their own posts; board-level moderation controls allow designated admins to remove content. Threads sort by latest activity; posts are chronological within a thread. Posts support basic formatting (markdown or simple HTML). Exercises: shared mutable state across users, authentication and per-user permissions, real-time updates from other users, threading/nesting, rich text input, moderation controls.

### 5. Knowledge Base

A personal wiki for organizing notes, ideas, and reference material. Each entry has a title, rich text body (headings, bold, italic, lists, code blocks), tags, and creation/modification timestamps. Entries can link to other entries via wiki-style cross-references (`[[Entry Title]]`), forming a navigable graph. A backlinks section on each entry shows all entries that reference it. Full-text search across all entries. Exercises: rich text editing, cross-referencing and link resolution, backlink computation, tagging, full-text search, deep content hierarchy.

### 6. Bookmark Manager


A hierarchical bookmark organizer with folders, tags, and full-text search. Each bookmark has a URL, title, description, tags, and a timestamp. Folders can nest arbitrarily. Bookmarks are drag-reorderable within folders. Supports import from a simple format. Exercises: recursive hierarchy (nested folders), tagging system, full-text search, URL validation, drag-to-reorder, bulk import, deep navigation.

## Study Design

### Environment

Each implementation starts from the same written specification. The LLM receives the app spec and the relevant framework documentation (STRVCT docs or React/library docs) and builds the app through iterative prompting. No human code review or correction during the build -- the LLM debugs its own errors.

### Metrics

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Prompt rounds | Number of user→LLM turns to reach a working app |
| Debug iterations | Turns spent fixing errors vs. building new features |
| Token usage | Total input + output tokens consumed |
| Lines of code | Final app size excluding framework/library code |
| File count | Number of source files in the final app |
| ARIA coverage | Percentage of interactive elements with correct ARIA roles and states |
| Persistence + sync code | Lines dedicated to storage and cloud sync (annotations vs. explicit read/write) |
| Feature addition | Effort to add a specified new feature after initial completion |

### Controls

- Same app spec, same acceptance criteria
- Same LLM model (or multiple models run independently)
- React stack chosen to be representative, not strawman: current React with hooks, a mainstream router, and a widely-used component library
- React implementations may use any third-party libraries (drag-and-drop, Firebase SDK, accessibility utilities) -- the total effort including library integration is part of the measurement
- Each app tested against the same manual test checklist

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Cleanup Notes -->
Source: docs/Plans/Cleanup%20Notes/

# Cleanup Notes

Areas of the codebase that work but could benefit from simplification, documentation, or restructuring.

**Status:** open; checked against the source 2026-11-13. Done since the first draft: Notification Center indexing (`tests/headless/TestNotificationIndexes.js`) and the `isInTx()` question in the object pool. Moved: view compaction to [Browser Cleanup](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/), model/view items to [Naked Objects Issues](docs/Plans/Naked%20Objects%20Issues/), schema migration to its own entry in the [Meta Plan](docs/Plans/Meta%20Plan/).

The runtime-risk items are done; the rest are for when a file is being changed anyway. When rewriting a file, re-check the fixes already applied to it (see the framework guide on diagnostics coming back in rewrites).

## Can Fail at Runtime

Both items here are fixed (2026-11-15):

- **ObjectPool recursive GC.** `markPid()` (`SvObjectPool_collection.js`) walks with an explicit stack; a chain of 300,000 references marks without overflowing (`tests/headless/TestGcDeepReferenceChain.js`).
- **Promise-wrapped slot errors.** A failed computation is no longer cached. See [Promise-Wrapped Slots](docs/Plans/Promise-Wrapped%20Slots/#error-recovery).

## Structure

### Slot Hooks

`Slot.js` (2,295 lines) has a TODO: "hooks code is a mess, need to cleanup and modularize." The hook system (`onWillGet`, `onDidUpdate`, `onUndefinedGet`, …) is set up across scattered code paths, and the file also holds storage configuration, inspector settings, validation, JSON Schema and lazy loading.

Splitting it into categories (`Slot_hooks.js`, `Slot_storage.js`, `Slot_inspection.js`, `Slot_lazy.js`) would separate concerns without changing the public API; `Slot_promiseWrapper.js` already shows the shape.

### SvCssDomView

`SvCssDomView.js` (2,993 lines) holds 100+ CSS property accessors, plus commented-out code: a push/pop attribute stack and an `applyCSS` helper.

- **Group the accessors** into categories (`SvCssDomView_layout.js`, `SvCssDomView_typography.js`, …), or generate the repetitive ones from a property list.
- **Remove the commented-out code.** Git keeps it.

### Notification Names

Notification names (`onStackViewPathChangeNote`, `onRequestNavigateToNode`, …) are string literals scattered through the code. A pass could:

- Collect them as constants on the classes that post them.
- Document which classes post and which observe each.
- Find the ones no longer posted or observed.

### View Class Discovery

Discovery by naming convention (`Contact` → `ContactTile`) is surprising when it doesn't find a match. A debug log, or an inspector field, showing which view class was chosen for a node and why would help.

### Boot Loader Ordering

`SvBootLoader.js` loads its files from a hardcoded array whose order matters, with the dependencies recorded only in comments ("important that this be after SvIndexedDbFolder/Tx"). An explicit dependency list or a check at boot would let it validate its own order.

### IndexedDB Browser/Server Duplication

`SvIndexedDbFolder.js` exists in `browser-only/` (871 lines) and `server-only/` (483), as does `SvIndexedDbTx.js` (445 and 438). A shared base would shrink the surface and keep the two consistent.

### Resource Manager and the Loading View

`SvResourceManager.js` calls `SvBootLoadingView` directly to update progress. Posting progress notifications instead would let the loading view observe them, and keep the loader free of UI.

### Error Handling

Errors are reported in several ways: `console.error()` with emoji prefixes, context added to error objects (`evalError.evalPath = path`), custom error classes (`SvJsonPatchError`, `SvMissingSlotError`, the AI request errors), and catch-and-log. A convention for which to use when would make errors easier to trace.

### Hand-Kept Promises

Most code that kept its own `fooPromise` for work several callers ask for at once moved to [shared promises](docs/Programming%20Idioms/Async%20Patterns/index.html) (2026-11-15). Two copies are left in the framework:

- **`SvBlobPool`**: `activeReadsMap` / `activeWritesMap` are the one-at-a-time pattern keyed by hash. `inFlightPromiseNamed("read " + hash, …)` would do it, once it is checked that entries are forgotten on failure as they are now.
- **`SvWaSound.fetchPromise`**: a load done once.

Not candidates: a promise created empty and settled later by an event (`SvResource.loadDataPromise`, `SvWaContext.setupPromise`, `SvDatabase.setupPromise`, `SvRzSigServerConn.connectPromise`, the `completionPromise` slots).

### Theme Value Generation

`SvThemeState`'s value lists (`validLetterSpacingValues()` and its siblings) are rebuilt on every call, 50+ strings each. Compute them once per class.

## Noise

### Commented-Out Code

- `SvJsonGroup.js`: the `hasBeenLoaded` slot and lazy-loading scaffolding, superseded by [Lazy Slots](docs/Plans/Lazy%20Slots/).
- `SvStorableNode.js`: the commented-out `setIsLazy(true)` ("no point in using this until we have coroutines"), also superseded.
- `SvCssDomView.js`: the push/pop attribute stack (above).
- `SvResourceManager.js`: an alternative parallel loading approach.
- `SvNode_subnodes.js`: two "TODO: remove after debugging" lines.

### Unused Files

107 files sit in 33 `_unused/` folders across the source tree. They're out of the build, but they turn up in every search. Delete them (git keeps them) or move them to one archive folder.

### Stale TODOs

There are 140 TODO/FIXME comments in `source/` (not counting `_unused/` and `external-libs/`). Some are stale: "hasOwnProperty?" questions in `Slot.js` that `Object.hasOwn()` already answers, debug leftovers, and bare `// TODO:` with no description. A pass to resolve or explain them would make the rest useful as a backlog.

<!-- Page: docs/Plans/Compaction Coordinator -->
Source: docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/

# Compaction Coordinator

The rules for which columns a browser shows and how wide each is, gathered into one place that can be tested without a browser.

**Status:** **parts A to D are released to production** (2026-11-22, app PR #788, on Steve's word; parts C and D had no outside review). Built: part A (A1, A2, A3, A4, A7), the thumbnail fix, part B's timings (compaction is under the 2ms line, so C rested on testability), part C (claims in the views, allocation in `SvLayerAllocation`) and three part D changes; see the "as built" sections below. Where the text says "on dev, not released", that was true when written. **Open:** the rest of part D, each when a case needs it; the questions in [For the next pass](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#for-the-next-pass), which a review of C and D should answer; and the companion, whose code is kept with nothing spent on it until a node uses one (decision 17). It is part 2 of [Browser Cleanup](docs/Plans/Browser%20Cleanup/). The decisions, dated, are in [Decisions](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#decisions). A review of this page was folded in six times on 2026-11-20 and 2026-11-21 (the reviewer's file was removed on 2026-11-23, with the work finished for now; its answers are in the last section); what each pass changed is marked "(review)" and "(review 2)" to "(review 6)".

**What changed from the first draft (2026-11-19).** That draft proposed a layout object, `SvColumnLayout`, that was handed a flat list of columns and answered with a plan. The review found three things it had not taken in: the levels are nested inside each other, not laid side by side; each level chooses its own direction; and an object that solved the whole layout would have to repeat what the views already know about themselves. This version keeps each view's knowledge in the view and moves only the arithmetic. It also puts the small, safe fixes first and a measurement before the larger change.

## Compaction in the lens model

The [Naked Objects](docs/Naked%20Objects/) paper describes a screen as a lens over the model, made of three decisions: which nodes are **visible**, whether each visible parent-to-child edge is **layered** (the child gets its own plane, beside or in front of its parent) or **inlined** (the child is drawn within its parent's extent), and how siblings are **arranged**. It says the framework owns the mechanics, and names one of them: *responsive collapse is the lens switching edges from inlined to layered as space runs out, within the bounds the hints allow.*

That mechanic is what this plan is about. Read that way, the code has four separate implementations of it, one per kind of edge:

| What the user sees | In the lens model | Where it is decided today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earlier columns hide and the breadcrumbs keep the path | Layers stacked in depth, no longer side by side. Still layered. | `SvStackView` and `SvNavView` |
| A docked companion becomes a tab | An inlined edge becomes layered | `SvDetailView` and `SvCompanionView` |
| Side-by-side panes become tabs | An inlined edge becomes layered | `SvAnchoredTabsLayout` |
| A document's sections go from three text columns to one; a section folds to a tile | Inlined siblings rearranged; an inlined edge becomes layered, by the user's hand | CSS, and `SvInlineSectionTile` |

A pin on a companion or a tab, and a folded section, are the same thing too: the user choosing a placement, inside what the hints allow.

So the destination is one protocol in which every edge says how it wants to be placed, how far it may give way, and how much room it needs. It is a shared protocol and not one owner. Part C is the first step: the layers, with each companion's reservation handed in as a number by the companion that worked it out. `SvAnchoredTabsLayout` stays the owner of its panes for good: two panes with the same claim can need different answers, because a player dragged their divider, chose a different member of a group, or closed a pane that should be the first to come back. What it shares with the rest is the edge of the protocol: its reservation goes outward, the width it is given comes inward, and it divides that width by the history it keeps. (review 2) What this page calls a *level* is a layer in the paper's words.

## What compaction does today

### The structure

A browser shows a chain of levels. Each level is a `SvStackView` holding a nav view (the column or menu) and a detail view. The detail view holds **the next level's whole stack**, and that level's companion panel if it has one. So the levels are nested: the third column is inside the second level's detail view, which is inside the first's. The one place views sit side by side is an anchored-tabs level, whose panes are siblings.

**An anchored-tabs level ends its browser's chain.** Each open pane is a browser of its own, with its own chain, laid out against the width of its pane's frame. So there are two calculations there, not one: the outer chain, in which the anchored level reserves width and the columns before it give way, and each pane's chain, in which the pane's columns fit the pane. (review)

Each level takes its direction from its node:

- `"right"`: the nav is a column on the left and the next level is beside it.
- `"down"`: the nav is a row across the top and the next level is beneath it.

**No node in the app supplies a companion today.** `nodeCompanionNode()` answers null in the framework and nothing in the app overrides it; the Narration and Party panels that were companions are now anchored tabs, each pane a browser of its own. The companion panel is exercised only by the framework's own spec, which supplies one at run time. So every companion rule on this page is a rule of the framework that no player reaches, and what that means for C's scope is a question for Steve under [Still open](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#still-open). (review 3)

In the app today every node is `"right"`, the default. The only `"down"` levels in use are anchored tabs, which force it. Any other direction throws. `"left"` and `"up"` are wanted eventually, `"left"` for right-to-left languages among other uses; see [Four directions](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#four-directions).

A level also chooses how it shows its children (`nodeChildrenLayout()`): one per tile in a column, as anchored tabs, or **inline**, where the next levels are laid out in place as a document (Inline Navigation, in the app's plans). So a level is not always a column, and one column can hold several levels of the tree. See [Inline documents](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#inline-documents).

### The rules

- Only `"right"` levels take part. A `"down"` level is never hidden and adds no width, since its row costs height and the levels beneath it get its full width.
- A column is hidden when its target width, plus the target widths of every `"right"` column after it, plus every docked companion and anchored-tabs claim after it, is not less than the root width. So columns give way from the left.
- A column that fills the leftover width (a narration, an inline document) is never hidden. It shrinks. Only the last column can be a fill column.
- A companion's room is the root width minus its own level's column, and nothing else. It docks when its preferred length fits, becomes a tab when it doesn't, and is hidden when even the tab doesn't fit. A user's pin wins while the tab fits.
- A companion's mode and its docked length are worked out from different budgets. The mode uses the column's comfortable target. The length may grow, for the width hint of the node in focus, into the room above the column's yield floor. A pin to docked keeps the panel at **at least** its preferred length whenever the tab fits, even when that is more than the room; a larger hint can still widen it. (review, review 2)
- Hidden means `display: none`. A column does not animate. A companion does: its size changes over 380ms, and its embedded browser is laid out again 400ms after it docks. So a companion's reservation is at its new value while its box is still narrower, and a recording has to take three things apart: the reservation when it is decided, the box in transition, and the box once settled. Otherwise a correct frame in between reads as a wrong answer. (review 4)

The arithmetic is **flat**: every comparison is against the root width, although the views are nested. It gives the right answer because columns give way strictly from the left.

A column's target width is the larger of 270px and its node's `nodeMinTileWidth()`, plus a thumbnail allowance, capped at the available width.

## Where it lives

| Class | Its part |
| --- | --- |
| `SvStackView` | Sums the widths after it, decides hide or show for its own column, and loops the whole chain until nothing changes. |
| `SvNavView` | Target width, available width, hide and show, and the width styles. |
| `SvDetailView` | A companion's room. |
| `SvCompanionView` | Docked, tab or hidden, and its docked length. |
| `SvStackView_anchoredTabs` | How much width the panes claim. |

## What is wrong with it

Each was read from the source. None has been measured in a browser; part B does that.

1. **It runs far more often than the layout changes.** Every stack's `syncFromNode` ends in a pass over the whole chain. A node update bubbles to the root, so a streamed narration runs it for every level on every chunk.
2. **Every level answers a window resize.** Each stack registers for the event and each recompacts the whole chain: N passes per event, each looping up to five times. The source has a TODO saying only the top stack should register.
3. **The pass loops because of its order.** Each level decides its column first and its companion second, so a column reads companion states left over from the pass before. Deciding companions first and columns second needs one pass, since a companion's room does not depend on which columns are hidden.
4. **Three names for one method.** `safeUpdateCompactionChain`, `updateCompactionChain` and `recompactBrowserChain`, with 12 call sites.
5. **The width styles are written twice, and disagree.** `SvNavView.makeOrientationRight` and `SvNavView.updateWidthForWindow` hold near-copies of one rule. The second has a case the first lacks: the last column fills the row when the root is between one and two column widths. In that case every sync writes the fixed width and then the full width.
6. **A height is measured on every pass.** A bottom-edge companion's room is read from `clientHeight` inside the loop, after widths are written. It is a raw element read, so the thrash counter does not see it.
7. **Views ask the window, not the layout.** `SvOptionNodeTile` decides whether to step back after a pick by comparing the window width with 540. What it wants to know is whether its parent column is hidden.
8. **Numbers without names.** 270, `17em`, 540, 200, and the loop guard of five.
9. **No test holds the rules.** The anchored tabs have `TestAnchoredTabsLayout`. The columns have nothing like it, so every fix so far was found in a browser and guarded by a comment.

## Recommendation

In this order: the recordings, part A, the thumbnail fix, part B, and then part C if B's numbers call for it. Everything before C is small and worth doing whatever is decided about C.

### Before part A: record what the fixes must not change (review)

Part A is meant to change nothing a user sees, so what it could change is recorded first. **Steve has said to start these (2026-11-20), with one condition: not everything the columns do today is how they should behave.** So a recording says what happens, not what is right. Its assertions are named as today's behaviour, anything that looks wrong is listed for Steve with the recording, and a behaviour he calls wrong is taken out of what part A and part C must reproduce and becomes a fix of its own.

- **Mend the width spec.** `app-mobile-column-width.spec.js` asserts on the widest ancestor of the "My Sessions" tile. A wrapper as wide as the viewport passes it while the column itself is stuck at 270px. It should measure the enclosing nav view.
- **Record a window resize** before A1, counting calls to the chain pass apart from the loops inside each call.
- *Deferred with the companion (Steve, 2026-11-20):* the bottom-edge companion's height changing, and two side companions in one chain. The reviewer built both fixtures in Chromium from plain `SvSummaryNode`s and the `nodeCompanionNode()` hook, and what they saw is kept here for when the companion is taken up. Bottom edge, on a host with `setNodeIsVertical(false)` at a width of 1,000px: hidden at a detail height of 219px, a tab from 220px to 579px, docked from 580px, no width reserved. Two side companions, each asking for 700px at a 1,000px root with three 270px columns: both dock and reserve 700px, the first two columns hide and the third shows; at 600px both are tabs and reserve nothing. `companion-panel.spec.js` accepts a tab while requiring a reservation above zero, which should depend on the mode. (review 4)
- **Record a narration that asks for 900px in a 390px pane**, after an ordinary node update, beside a column that is not a fill column and has stretched to fill the row. This is before A3, which touches the rule next to the one that fixed that narration. (review 2)
- **Record the solo Party sheet**, as the last column and with a tile opened from it. The Party tab asks for 437px and, for a party of one, presents a sheet that asks for 300px, so it is the case in which the two nodes disagree (see [Two fixes that are decisions](docs/Plans/Compaction%20Coordinator/#two-fixes-that-are-decisions)).

#### What the recordings show (2026-11-20, on dev)

Taken by `tests/e2e/compaction-recordings.spec.js` in the app repo, which writes `tests/e2e/recordings/compaction-before-A.json`: one new session with one character seated, 41 steps, no page errors. It has been taken three times. The numbers here are the second run's, taken after the GM's opening had finished arriving (see point 2 below), and that run is the baseline (app commit 5e57446e4). The reviewer compared the first two runs: the same open tabs and the same stack states at all 32 steps of the resize. The third run matched the baseline in layout at every step and in every pass count (292 calls, 530 level visits, 212 resize handlers). `app-mobile-column-width.spec.js` is mended and passes. Nothing below is asserted as right.

**The width spec was measuring nothing.** On a phone the "My Sessions" text it looked for is the breadcrumb, not a tile, so none of its ancestors was a column. It now reads the columns: the root column hidden, the My Sessions column 393px of 393px.

**The session at 1,600px.** The app's two columns (the root and My Sessions) are hidden and the session's tab row takes the full width. Narration alone is 1,600px. With Party opened, Narration is 1,076px and Party 522px. Both panes' columns are fill columns.

**The resize.** Both panes stay open down to 1,040px (Narration 602px, Party 436px). At 1,000px and below only Party shows, at the full width, and Narration is closed. Coming back up, Narration returns at 1,040px. This agrees with the reviewer's 1,038px.

**The Narration column at 390px.** It is 390px wide, a fill column with no minimum, before and after an ordinary node update on the chat. The narration that asks for 900px does not overflow.

**The solo Party sheet.** The Party column's own node asks for 437px and the sheet it presents for 300px, as read. At every width recorded it is a fill column, so the difference never shows. **The second case could not be taken:** no tile on a new character's sheet opens past the inlined levels, so there was nothing to open from inside it. That case, and the repeated section column, need a character with something to open, or the Inline Lab.

**Passes.** Script time in the passes only; the layout they cause is not in these numbers, and nothing was streaming.

| What happened | Calls to the chain pass | Level visits inside them | Resize handlers | Script time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One step of the resize (31 of the 32) | 7 to 9 | 13 to 17 | 6 or 7 | 0.2 to 0.7ms |
| The one step where Narration's pane reopens (1,000px to 1,040px) | 12 | 20 | 6 | 0.6ms |
| 1.2 seconds with nobody touching anything | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Opening the Party tab | 16 | 34 | 0 | 0.8ms |
| An ordinary node update on the chat | 6 | 14 | 0 | 0.3ms |

So one resize runs six or seven handlers, and one explicit node update on the chat runs six passes. The handlers are counted across the outer browser and its pane browsers together, so "where one would do" is not yet shown: it may be one per browser. A1 checks which stack answers a resize within its own browser, and that the panes still close and reopen. The script cost is small: a third of a millisecond for the node update. If the layout cost is as small, part B will find compaction under the 2ms line and C will rest on testability. That is a first sign and not part B's answer. (review 5)

**For Steve: things that happen today and may not be wanted.**

1. **Below about 1,038px, opening Party takes Narration's place**, and the tabs swap between the two. **Steve looked at the pictures and this is fine (2026-11-20).** I had called the sheet "stretched" at that width; it is not. At 1,000px it flows into two columns, the portrait beside the sections, and reads well. The pictures are taken by `tests/e2e/compaction-looks.spec.js` into `test-results/compaction-looks/`.
2. **Probably the narration, and not a fault of the resize.** In the first run some steps of the resize cost several times the others (47 calls at 700px going down, against 7 in the second run). The GM's opening was still arriving in the first run and had finished in the second, where every step is 7 to 9 calls but the one reopening, and an idle second is none. So streaming is the likely cause. It is not proved: the recorder counts no chunks, and I was wrong to say the extra calls came in multiples of six. What a streamed chunk costs is still open, and part B answers it by counting chunks against calls. (review 5)
3. **Nothing on a new fighter's sheet, or on the Inline Lab, opens past the inlined levels.** Rows with a description open in place. So the repeated section column the reviewer saw in a fixture is not something I could reach in the app, and it stays a case for a fixture. A sheet with spells or a long inventory was not tried.

#### The width rule before A3 (review 5)
